L4: cite1†SageMaker AI input modes and AWS cloud storage options L5: # Setting up training jobs to access datasets
L6: 
L7: When creating a training job, you specify the location of training datasets in a data storage of your choice and the data input mode for the job. Amazon SageMaker AI supports Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS), and Amazon FSx for Lustre. You can choose one of the input modes to stream the dataset in real time or download the whole dataset at the start of the training job.
L8: ###### Note
L9: 
L10: Your dataset must reside in the same AWS Region as the training job.
L11: ## SageMaker AI input modes and AWS cloud storage options
L12: 
L13: This section provides an overview of the file input modes supported by SageMaker for data stored in Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx for Lustre.
L14: 
L15: cite2†Image: Summary of the SageMaker AI input modes for Amazon S3 and file systems in Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx for Lustre. L16:   * File mode presents a file system view of the dataset to the training container. This is the default input mode if you don't explicitly specify one of the other two options. If you use file mode, SageMaker AI downloads the training data from the storage location to a local directory in the Docker container. Training starts after the full dataset has been downloaded. In file mode, the training instance must have enough storage space to fit the entire dataset.
L17: File mode download speed depends on the size of dataset, the average size of files, and the number of files. You can configure the dataset for file mode by providing either an Amazon S3 prefix, manifest file, or augmented manifest file. You should use an S3 prefix when all your dataset files are located within a common S3 prefix. File mode is compatible with cite3†SageMaker AI local mode†sagemaker.readthedocs.io (starting a SageMaker training container interactively in seconds).
L18: For distributed training, you can shard the dataset across multiple instances with the `ShardedByS3Key` option.
L19:   * Fast file mode provides file system access to an Amazon S3 data source while leveraging the performance advantage of pipe mode. At the start of training, fast file mode identifies the data files but does not download them. Training can start without waiting for the entire dataset to download. This means that the training startup takes less time when there are fewer files in the Amazon S3 prefix provided.
L20: In contrast to pipe mode, fast file mode works with random access to the data. However, it works best when data is read sequentially. Fast file mode doesn't support augmented manifest files.
L21: Fast file mode exposes S3 objects using a POSIX-compliant file system interface, as if the files are available on the local disk of your training instance. It streams S3 content on demand as your training script consumes data. This means that your dataset no longer needs to fit into the training instance storage space as a whole, and you don't need to wait for the dataset to be downloaded to the training instance before training starts.
L22: Fast file currently supports S3 prefixes only (it does not support manifest and augmented manifest). Fast file mode is compatible with SageMaker AI local mode.
L23: ###### Note
L24: 
L25: Using Fast File mode might lead to increased CloudTrail costs due to additional logging of:
L26: 
L27:     * Amazon S3 data events (if enabled in CloudTrail).
L28: 
L29:     * AWS KMS decryption events when accessing Amazon S3 objects encrypted with AWS KMS keys.
L30: 
L31:     * Management events related to AWS KMS operations.
L32: 
L33: Review your CloudTrail configuration and monitoring costs if you have CloudTrail logging enabled for these event types.
L34:   * Pipe mode streams data directly from an Amazon S3 data source. Streaming can provide faster start times and better throughput than file mode.
L35: 
L36: When you stream the data directly, you can reduce the size of the Amazon EBS volumes used by the training instance. Pipe mode needs only enough disk space to store the final model artifacts.
L37: It is another streaming mode that is largely replaced by the newer and simpler-to-use fast file mode. In pipe mode, data is pre-fetched from Amazon S3 at high concurrency and throughput, and streamed into a named pipe, which also known as a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) pipe for its behavior. Each pipe may only be read by a single process.
L38: A SageMaker AI specific extension to TensorFlow conveniently cite3†integrates Pipe mode into the native TensorFlow data loader†sagemaker.readthedocs.io for streaming text, TFRecords, or RecordIO file formats. Pipe mode also supports managed sharding and shuffling of data.
L39:   * Amazon S3 Express One Zone is a high-performance, single Availability Zone storage class that can deliver consistent, single-digit millisecond data access for the most latency-sensitive applications including SageMaker model training. Amazon S3 Express One Zone allows customers to collocate their object storage and compute resources in a single AWS Availability Zone, optimizing both compute performance and costs with increased data processing speed.
L40: To further increase access speed and support hundreds of thousands of requests per second, data is stored in a new bucket type, an Amazon S3 directory bucket.
L41: SageMaker AI model training supports high-performance Amazon S3 Express One Zone directory buckets as a data input location for file mode, fast file mode, and pipe mode. To use Amazon S3 Express One Zone, input the location of the Amazon S3 Express One Zone directory bucket instead of an Amazon S3 bucket. Provide the ARN for the IAM role with the required access control and permissions policy. Refer to cite4†AmazonSageMakerFullAccesspolicy for details.
L42: You can only encrypt your SageMaker AI output data in directory buckets with server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) is not currently supported for storing SageMaker AI output data in directory buckets. For more information, see cite5†Amazon S3 Express One Zone .
L43:   * Amazon FSx for Lustre – FSx for Lustre can scale to hundreds of gigabytes of throughput and millions of IOPS with low-latency file retrieval. When starting a training job, SageMaker AI mounts the FSx for Lustre file system to the training instance file system, then starts your training script. Mounting itself is a relatively fast operation that doesn't depend on the size of the dataset stored in FSx for Lustre.
L44: To access FSx for Lustre, your training job must connect to an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), which requires DevOps setup and involvement. To avoid data transfer costs, the file system uses a single Availability Zone, and you need to specify a VPC subnet which maps to this Availability Zone ID when running the training job.
L45:   * Amazon EFS – To use Amazon EFS as a data source, the data must already reside in Amazon EFS prior to training. SageMaker AI mounts the specified Amazon EFS file system to the training instance, then starts your training script. Your training job must connect to a VPC to access Amazon EFS.
L46: ###### Tip
L47: 
L48: To learn more about how to specify your VPC configuration to SageMaker AI ModelTrainers, see cite6†Use File Systems as Training Inputs†sagemaker.readthedocs.io in the SageMaker AI Python SDK documentation.

L2: XGBoost hyperparameters - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: # XGBoost hyperparameters
L4: The following table contains the subset of hyperparameters that are required or most commonly used for the Amazon SageMaker AI XGBoost algorithm. These are parameters that are set by users to facilitate the estimation of model parameters from data. The required hyperparameters that must be set are listed first, in alphabetical order. The optional hyperparameters that can be set are listed next, also in alphabetical order.
L5: The SageMaker AI XGBoost algorithm is an implementation of the open-source DMLC XGBoost package. For details about full set of hyperparameter that can be configured for this version of XGBoost, see cite1†XGBoost Parameters†xgboost.readthedocs.io .
L6: Parameter Name  | Description
L7: --- | ---
L8: `num_class`  | The number of classes. Required if `objective` is set to multi:softmax or multi:softprob. Valid values: Integer.
L9: `num_round`  | The number of rounds to run the training. Required Valid values: Integer.
L10: `alpha`  | L1 regularization term on weights. Increasing this value makes models more conservative. Optional Valid values: Float. Default value: 0
L11: `base_score`  | The initial prediction score of all instances, global bias. Optional Valid values: Float. Default value: 0.5
L12: `booster`  | Which booster to use. The `gbtree` and `dart` values use a tree-based model, while `gblinear` uses a linear function. Optional Valid values: String. One of `"gbtree"`, `"gblinear"`, or `"dart"`. Default value: `"gbtree"`
L13: `colsample_bylevel`  | Subsample ratio of columns for each split, in each level. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: [0,1]. Default value: 1
L14: `colsample_bynode`  | Subsample ratio of columns from each node. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: (0,1]. Default value: 1
L15: `colsample_bytree`  | Subsample ratio of columns when constructing each tree. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: [0,1]. Default value: 1
L16: `csv_weights`  | When this flag is enabled, XGBoost differentiates the importance of instances for csv input by taking the second column (the column after labels) in training data as the instance weights. Optional Valid values: 0 or 1 Default value: 0
L17: `deterministic_histogram`  | When this flag is enabled, XGBoost builds histogram on GPU deterministically. Used only if `tree_method` is set to `gpu_hist`. For a full list of valid inputs, please refer to cite2†XGBoost Parameters†github.com . Optional Valid values: String. Range: `"true"` or `"false"`. Default value: `"true"`
L18: `early_stopping_rounds`  | The model trains until the validation score stops improving. Validation error needs to decrease at least every `early_stopping_rounds` to continue training. SageMaker AI hosting uses the best model for inference. Optional Valid values: Integer. Default value: -
L19: `eta`  | Step size shrinkage used in updates to prevent overfitting. After each boosting step, you can directly get the weights of new features. The `eta` parameter actually shrinks the feature weights to make the boosting process more conservative. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: [0,1]. Default value: 0.3
L20: `eval_metric`  | Evaluation metrics for validation data. A default metric is assigned according to the objective:
L21:   * `rmse`: for regression
L22:   * `error`: for classification
L23:   * `map`: for ranking
L24: For a list of valid inputs, see cite3†XGBoost Learning Task Parameters†github.com . Optional Valid values: String. Default value: Default according to objective.
L25: `gamma`  | Minimum loss reduction required to make a further partition on a leaf node of the tree. The larger, the more conservative the algorithm is. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: [0,∞). Default value: 0
L26: `grow_policy`  | Controls the way that new nodes are added to the tree. Currently supported only if `tree_method` is set to `hist`. Optional Valid values: String. Either `"depthwise"` or `"lossguide"`. Default value: `"depthwise"`
L27: `interaction_constraints`  | Specify groups of variables that are allowed to interact. Optional Valid values: Nested list of integers. Each integer represents a feature, and each nested list contains features that are allowed to interact e.g., [[1,2], [3,4,5]]. Default value: None
L28: `lambda`  | L2 regularization term on weights. Increasing this value makes models more conservative. Optional Valid values: Float. Default value: 1
L29: `lambda_bias`  | L2 regularization term on bias. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: [0.0, 1.0]. Default value: 0
L30: `max_bin`  | Maximum number of discrete bins to bucket continuous features. Used only if `tree_method` is set to `hist`. Optional Valid values: Integer. Default value: 256
L31: `max_delta_step`  | Maximum delta step allowed for each tree's weight estimation. When a positive integer is used, it helps make the update more conservative. The preferred option is to use it in logistic regression. Set it to 1-10 to help control the update. Optional Valid values: Integer. Range: [0,∞). Default value: 0
L32: `max_depth`  | Maximum depth of a tree. Increasing this value makes the model more complex and likely to be overfit. 0 indicates no limit. A limit is required when `grow_policy`=`depth-wise`. Optional Valid values: Integer. Range: [0,∞) Default value: 6
L33: `max_leaves`  | Maximum number of nodes to be added. Relevant only if `grow_policy` is set to `lossguide`. Optional Valid values: Integer. Default value: 0
L34: `min_child_weight`  | Minimum sum of instance weight (hessian) needed in a child. If the tree partition step results in a leaf node with the sum of instance weight less than `min_child_weight`, the building process gives up further partitioning. In linear regression models, this simply corresponds to a minimum number of instances needed in each node. The larger the algorithm, the more conservative it is. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: [0,∞). Default value: 1
L35: `monotone_constraints`  | Specifies monotonicity constraints on any feature. Optional Valid values: Tuple of Integers. Valid integers: -1 (decreasing constraint), 0 (no constraint), 1 (increasing constraint). E.g., (0, 1): No constraint on first predictor, and an increasing constraint on the second. (-1, 1): Decreasing constraint on first predictor, and an increasing constraint on the second. Default value: (0, 0)
L36: `normalize_type`  | Type of normalization algorithm. Optional Valid values: Either tree or forest. Default value: tree
L37: `nthread`  | Number of parallel threads used to run xgboost. Optional Valid values: Integer. Default value: Maximum number of threads.
L38: `objective`  | Specifies the learning task and the corresponding learning objective. Examples: `reg:logistic`, `multi:softmax`, `reg:squarederror`. For a full list of valid inputs, refer to cite3†XGBoost Learning Task Parameters†github.com . Optional Valid values: String Default value: `"reg:squarederror"`
L39: `one_drop`  | When this flag is enabled, at least one tree is always dropped during the dropout. Optional Valid values: 0 or 1 Default value: 0
L40: `process_type`  | The type of boosting process to run. Optional Valid values: String. Either `"default"` or `"update"`. Default value: `"default"`
L41: `rate_drop`  | The dropout rate that specifies the fraction of previous trees to drop during the dropout. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: [0.0, 1.0]. Default value: 0.0
L42: `refresh_leaf`  | This is a parameter of the 'refresh' updater plug-in. When set to `true` (1), tree leaves and tree node stats are updated. When set to `false`(0), only tree node stats are updated. Optional Valid values: 0/1 Default value: 1
L43: `sample_type`  | Type of sampling algorithm. Optional Valid values: Either `uniform` or `weighted`. Default value: `uniform`
L44: `scale_pos_weight`  | Controls the balance of positive and negative weights. It's useful for unbalanced classes. A typical value to consider: `sum(negative cases)` / `sum(positive cases)`. Optional Valid values: float Default value: 1
L45: `seed`  | Random number seed. Optional Valid values: integer Default value: 0
L46: `single_precision_histogram`  | When this flag is enabled, XGBoost uses single precision to build histograms instead of double precision. Used only if `tree_method` is set to `hist` or `gpu_hist`. For a full list of valid inputs, please refer to cite2†XGBoost Parameters†github.com . Optional Valid values: String. Range: `"true"` or `"false"` Default value: `"false"`
L47: `sketch_eps`  | Used only for approximate greedy algorithm. This translates into O(1 / `sketch_eps`) number of bins. Compared to directly select number of bins, this comes with theoretical guarantee with sketch accuracy. Optional Valid values: Float, Range: [0, 1]. Default value: 0.03
L48: `skip_drop`  | Probability of skipping the dropout procedure during a boosting iteration. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: [0.0, 1.0]. Default value: 0.0
L49: `subsample`  | Subsample ratio of the training instance. Setting it to 0.5 means that XGBoost randomly collects half of the data instances to grow trees. This prevents overfitting. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: [0,1]. Default value: 1
L50: `tree_method`  | The tree construction algorithm used in XGBoost. Optional Valid values: One of `auto`, `exact`, `approx`, `hist`, or `gpu_hist`. Default value: `auto`
L51: `tweedie_variance_power`  | Parameter that controls the variance of the Tweedie distribution. Optional Valid values: Float. Range: (1, 2). Default value: 1.5
L52: `updater`  | A comma-separated string that defines the sequence of tree updaters to run. This provides a modular way to construct and to modify the trees. For a full list of valid inputs, please refer to cite2†XGBoost Parameters†github.com . Optional Valid values: comma-separated string. Default value: `grow_colmaker`, prune
L53: `use_dask_gpu_training`  | Set `use_dask_gpu_training` to `"true"` if you want to run distributed GPU training with Dask. Dask GPU training is only supported for versions 1.5-1 and later. Do not set this value to `"true"` for versions preceding 1.5-1. For more information, see cite4†Distributed GPU training . Optional Valid values: String. Range: `"true"` or `"false"` Default value: `"false"`
L54: `verbosity`  | Verbosity of printing messages. Valid values: 0 (silent), 1 (warning), 2 (info), 3 (debug). Optional Default value: 1

L6: # Connect a Notebook Instance in a VPC to External Resources
L7: 
L8: The following topic gives information on how to connect your notebook instance in a VPC to external resources.
L9: ## Default communication with the internet
L10: When your notebook allows direct internet access, SageMaker AI provides a network interface that allows the notebook to communicate with the internet through a VPC managed by SageMaker AI. Traffic within your VPC's CIDR goes through elastic network interface created in your VPC. All the other traffic goes through the network interface created by SageMaker AI, which is essentially through the public internet.
L11: Traffic to gateway VPC endpoints like Amazon S3 and DynamoDB goes through the public internet, while traffic to interface VPC interface endpoints still goes through your VPC. If you want to use gateway VPC endpoints, you might want to disable direct internet access.
L12: ## VPC-only communication with the internet
L13: 
L14: To disable direct internet access, you can specify a VPC for your notebook instance. By doing so, you prevent SageMaker AI from providing internet access to your notebook instance. As a result, the notebook instance can't train or host models unless your VPC has an interface endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) or a NAT gateway and your security groups allow outbound connections.
L15: For information about creating a VPC interface endpoint to use AWS PrivateLink for your notebook instance, see cite4†Connect to a Notebook Instance Through a VPC Interface Endpoint . For information about setting up a NAT gateway for your VPC, see cite5†VPC with Public and Private Subnets (NAT) in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud User Guide. For information about security groups, see cite6†Security Groups for Your VPC .
L16: For more information about networking configurations in each networking mode and configuring network on premise, see cite7†Understanding Amazon SageMaker notebook instance networking configurations and advanced routing options†aws.amazon.com .
L17: ###### Warning
L18: 
L19: When you use a VPC for your notebook instance, you partly own the networking configuration for the instance. As a security best practice, we recommend that you apply least-privilege permissions to the inbound and outbound access that you permit with your security group rules. If you apply overly permissive inbound rule configurations, then users who have access to your VPC could access your Jupyter Notebooks without authenticating.
L20: ## Security and Shared Notebook Instances
L21: 
L22: A SageMaker notebook instance is designed to work best for an individual user. It is designed to give data scientists and other users the most power for managing their development environment.
L23: A notebook instance user has root access for installing packages and other pertinent software. We recommend that you exercise judgement when granting individuals access to notebook instances that are attached to a VPC that contains sensitive information. For example, you might grant a user access to a notebook instance with an IAM policy by giving them the ability to create a presigned notebook URL, as shown in the following example:
L24:

L29:         "Version":"2012-10-17",
L30:         "Statement": [
L31:             {
L32:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L33:                 "Action": "sagemaker:CreatePresignedNotebookInstanceUrl",
L34:                 "Resource": "arn:aws:sagemaker:`us-east-1`:`111122223333`:notebook-instance/myNotebookInstance"
L35:             }
L36:         ]
L37:     }`

L2: Use the SageMaker AI DeepAR forecasting algorithm - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Input/Output Interface for the DeepAR Algorithm cite2†Best Practices for Using the DeepAR Algorithm cite3†EC2 Instance Recommendations for the DeepAR Algorithm cite4†Sample Notebooks L5: # Use the SageMaker AI DeepAR forecasting algorithm
L6: 
L7: The Amazon SageMaker AI DeepAR forecasting algorithm is a supervised learning algorithm for forecasting scalar (one-dimensional) time series using recurrent neural networks (RNN). Classical forecasting methods, such as autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) or exponential smoothing (ETS), fit a single model to each individual time series. They then use that model to extrapolate the time series into the future.
L8: In many applications, however, you have many similar time series across a set of cross-sectional units. For example, you might have time series groupings for demand for different products, server loads, and requests for webpages. For this type of application, you can benefit from training a single model jointly over all of the time series. DeepAR takes this approach. When your dataset contains hundreds of related time series, DeepAR outperforms the standard ARIMA and ETS methods.
L9: You can also use the trained model to generate forecasts for new time series that are similar to the ones it has been trained on.
L10: The training input for the DeepAR algorithm is one or, preferably, more `target` time series that have been generated by the same process or similar processes. Based on this input dataset, the algorithm trains a model that learns an approximation of this process/processes and uses it to predict how the target time series evolves.
L11: Each target time series can be optionally associated with a vector of static (time-independent) categorical features provided by the `cat` field and a vector of dynamic (time-dependent) time series provided by the `dynamic_feat` field. SageMaker AI trains the DeepAR model by randomly sampling training examples from each target time series in the training dataset. Each training example consists of a pair of adjacent context and prediction windows with fixed predefined lengths.
L12: To control how far in the past the network can see, use the `context_length` hyperparameter. To control how far in the future predictions can be made, use the `prediction_length` hyperparameter. For more information, see cite5†How the DeepAR Algorithm Works .

L21:   * cite4†DeepAR Sample Notebooks L22: 
L23:   * cite5†How the DeepAR Algorithm Works L24: 
L25:   * cite6†DeepAR Hyperparameters L26: 
L27:   * cite7†Tune a DeepAR Model L28: 
L29:   * cite8†DeepAR Inference Formats L30: ## Input/Output Interface for the DeepAR Algorithm
L31: 
L32: DeepAR supports two data channels. The required `train` channel describes the training dataset. The optional `test` channel describes a dataset that the algorithm uses to evaluate model accuracy after training. You can provide training and test datasets in cite9†JSON Lines†jsonlines.org format. Files can be in gzip or cite10†Parquet†parquet.apache.org file format.
L33: When specifying the paths for the training and test data, you can specify a single file or a directory that contains multiple files, which can be stored in subdirectories. If you specify a directory, DeepAR uses all files in the directory as inputs for the corresponding channel, except those that start with a period (.) and those named _SUCCESS. This ensures that you can directly use output folders produced by Spark jobs as input channels for your DeepAR training jobs.
L34: By default, the DeepAR model determines the input format from the file extension (`.json`, `.json.gz`, or `.parquet`) in the specified input path. If the path does not end in one of these extensions, you must explicitly specify the format in the SDK for Python. Use the `content_type` parameter of the cite11†InputData†sagemaker.readthedocs.io class.
L35: 
L36: The records in your input files should contain the following fields:
L37:   * `start`—A string with the format `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`. The start timestamp can't contain time zone information.
L38: 
L39:   * `target`—An array of floating-point values or integers that represent the time series. You can encode missing values as `null` literals, or as `"NaN"` strings in JSON, or as `nan` floating-point values in Parquet.
L40:   * `dynamic_feat` (optional)—An array of arrays of floating-point values or integers that represents the vector of custom feature time series (dynamic features). If you set this field, all records must have the same number of inner arrays (the same number of feature time series). In addition, each inner array must be the same length as the associated `target` value plus `prediction_length`. Missing values are not supported in the features.
L41: For example, if target time series represents the demand of different products, an associated `dynamic_feat` might be a boolean time-series which indicates whether a promotion was applied (1) to the particular product or not (0):
L42: 
L43:     `{"start": ..., "target": [1, 5, 10, 2], "dynamic_feat": [[0, 1, 1, 0]]}`
L44:   * `cat` (optional)—An array of categorical features that can be used to encode the groups that the record belongs to. Categorical features must be encoded as a 0-based sequence of positive integers. For example, the categorical domain {R, G, B} can be encoded as {0, 1, 2}. All values from each categorical domain must be represented in the training dataset. That's because the DeepAR algorithm can forecast only for categories that have been observed during training.
L45: And, each categorical feature is embedded in a low-dimensional space whose dimensionality is controlled by the `embedding_dimension` hyperparameter. For more information, see cite6†DeepAR Hyperparameters .
L46: If you use a JSON file, it must be in cite9†JSON Lines†jsonlines.org format. For example:
L47: 
L48:     `{"start": "2009-11-01 00:00:00", "target": [4.3, "NaN", 5.1, ...], "cat": [0, 1], "dynamic_feat": [[1.1, 1.2, 0.5, ...]]}
L49:     {"start": "2012-01-30 00:00:00", "target": [1.0, -5.0, ...], "cat": [2, 3], "dynamic_feat": [[1.1, 2.05, ...]]}
L50:     {"start": "1999-01-30 00:00:00", "target": [2.0, 1.0], "cat": [1, 4], "dynamic_feat": [[1.3, 0.4]]}`
L51: In this example, each time series has two associated categorical features and one time series features.
L52: 
L53: For Parquet, you use the same three fields as columns. In addition, `"start"` can be the `datetime` type. You can compress Parquet files using gzip (`gzip`) or the Snappy compression library (`snappy`).
L54: If the algorithm is trained without `cat` and `dynamic_feat` fields, it learns a "global" model, that is a model that is agnostic to the specific identity of the target time series at inference time and is conditioned only on its shape.
L55: If the model is conditioned on the `cat` and `dynamic_feat` feature data provided for each time series, the prediction will probably be influenced by the character of time series with the corresponding `cat` features. For example, if the `target` time series represents the demand of clothing items, you can associate a two-dimensional `cat` vector that encodes the type of item (e.g. 0 = shoes, 1 = dress) in the first component and the color of an item (e.g. 0 = red, 1 = blue) in the second component.
L56: A sample input would look as follows:
L57: 
L58:     `{ "start": ..., "target": ..., "cat": [0, 0], ... } # red shoes
L59:     { "start": ..., "target": ..., "cat": [1, 1], ... } # blue dress`
L60: At inference time, you can request predictions for targets with `cat` values that are combinations of the `cat` values observed in the training data, for example:
L61: 
L62:     `{ "start": ..., "target": ..., "cat": [0, 1], ... } # blue shoes
L63:     { "start": ..., "target": ..., "cat": [1, 0], ... } # red dress`
L64: 
L65: The following guidelines apply to training data:
L66:   * The start time and length of the time series can differ. For example, in marketing, products often enter a retail catalog at different dates, so their start dates naturally differ. But all series must have the same frequency, number of categorical features, and number of dynamic features.
L67: 
L68:   * Shuffle the training file with respect to the position of the time series in the file. In other words, the time series should occur in random order in the file.
L69:   * Make sure to set the `start` field correctly. The algorithm uses the `start` timestamp to derive the internal features.
L70:   * If you use categorical features (`cat`), all time series must have the same number of categorical features. If the dataset contains the `cat` field, the algorithm uses it and extracts the cardinality of the groups from the dataset. By default, `cardinality` is `"auto"`. If the dataset contains the `cat` field, but you don't want to use it, you can disable it by setting `cardinality` to `""`. If a model was trained using a `cat` feature, you must include it for inference.
L71:   * If your dataset contains the `dynamic_feat` field, the algorithm uses it automatically. All time series have to have the same number of feature time series. The time points in each of the feature time series correspond one-to-one to the time points in the target. In addition, the entry in the `dynamic_feat` field should have the same length as the `target`. If the dataset contains the `dynamic_feat` field, but you don't want to use it, disable it by setting(`num_dynamic_feat` to `""`).
L72: If the model was trained with the `dynamic_feat` field, you must provide this field for inference. In addition, each of the features has to have the length of the provided target plus the `prediction_length`. In other words, you must provide the feature value in the future.
L73: If you specify optional test channel data, the DeepAR algorithm evaluates the trained model with different accuracy metrics. The algorithm calculates the root mean square error (RMSE) over the test data as follows:
L74: 
L75: cite12†Image: RMSE Formula: Sqrt(1/nT(Sum[i,t](y-hat(i,t)-y(i,t))^2)). L76: y_{i,t} is the true value of time series i at the time t. ŷ_{i,t} is the mean prediction. The sum is over all n time series in the test set and over the last Τ time points for each time series, where Τ corresponds to the forecast horizon. You specify the length of the forecast horizon by setting the `prediction_length` hyperparameter. For more information, see cite6†DeepAR Hyperparameters .
L77: In addition, the algorithm evaluates the accuracy of the forecast distribution using weighted quantile loss. For a quantile in the range [0, 1], the weighted quantile loss is defined as follows:
L78: 
L79: cite13†Image: Weighted quantile loss equation. L80: q_{i,t}^{(τ)} is the τ-quantile of the distribution that the model predicts. To specify which quantiles to calculate loss for, set the `test_quantiles` hyperparameter. In addition to these, the average of the prescribed quantile losses is reported as part of the training logs. For information, see cite6†DeepAR Hyperparameters .
L81: 
L82: For inference, DeepAR accepts JSON format and the following fields:
L83: 
L84:   * `"instances"`, which includes one or more time series in JSON Lines format
L85:   * A name of `"configuration"`, which includes parameters for generating the forecast
L86: 
L87: For more information, see cite8†DeepAR Inference Formats .
L88: ## Best Practices for Using the DeepAR Algorithm
L89: 
L90: When preparing your time series data, follow these best practices to achieve the best results:
L91:   * Except for when splitting your dataset for training and testing, always provide the entire time series for training, testing, and when calling the model for inference. Regardless of how you set `context_length`, don't break up the time series or provide only a part of it. The model uses data points further back than the value set in `context_length` for the lagged values feature.
L92:   * When tuning a DeepAR model, you can split the dataset to create a training dataset and a test dataset. In a typical evaluation, you would test the model on the same time series used for training, but on the future `prediction_length` time points that follow immediately after the last time point visible during training.
L93: You can create training and test datasets that satisfy this criteria by using the entire dataset (the full length of all time series that are available) as a test set and removing the last `prediction_length` points from each time series for training. During training, the model doesn't see the target values for time points on which it is evaluated during testing. During testing, the algorithm withholds the last `prediction_length` points of each time series in the test set and generates a prediction.
L94: Then it compares the forecast with the withheld values. You can create more complex evaluations by repeating time series multiple times in the test set, but cutting them at different endpoints. With this approach, accuracy metrics are averaged over multiple forecasts from different time points. For more information, see cite7†Tune a DeepAR Model .
L95:   * Avoid using very large values (>400) for the `prediction_length` because it makes the model slow and less accurate. If you want to forecast further into the future, consider aggregating your data at a lower frequency. For example, use `5min` instead of `1min`.
L96:   * Because lags are used, a model can look further back in the time series than the value specified for `context_length`. Therefore, you don't need to set this parameter to a large value. We recommend starting with the value that you used for `prediction_length`.
L97:   * We recommend training a DeepAR model on as many time series as are available. Although a DeepAR model trained on a single time series might work well, standard forecasting algorithms, such as ARIMA or ETS, might provide more accurate results. The DeepAR algorithm starts to outperform the standard methods when your dataset contains hundreds of related time series. Currently, DeepAR requires that the total number of observations available across all training time series is at least 300.
L98: ## EC2 Instance Recommendations for the DeepAR Algorithm
L99: 
L100: You can train DeepAR on both GPU and CPU instances and in both single and multi-machine settings. We recommend starting with a single CPU instance (for example, ml.c4.2xlarge or ml.c4.4xlarge), and switching to GPU instances and multiple machines only when necessary. Using GPUs and multiple machines improves throughput only for larger models (with many cells per layer and many layers) and for large mini-batch sizes (for example, greater than 512).
L101: For inference, DeepAR supports only CPU instances.
L102: Specifying large values for `context_length`, `prediction_length`, `num_cells`, `num_layers`, or `mini_batch_size` can create models that are too large for small instances. In this case, use a larger instance type or reduce the values for these parameters. This problem also frequently occurs when running hyperparameter tuning jobs. In that case, use an instance type large enough for the model tuning job and consider limiting the upper values of the critical parameters to avoid job failures.
L103: ## DeepAR Sample Notebooks
L104: For a sample notebook that shows how to prepare a time series dataset for training the SageMaker AI DeepAR algorithm and how to deploy the trained model for performing inferences, see cite14†DeepAR demo on electricity dataset†sagemaker-examples.readthedocs.io , which illustrates the advanced features of DeepAR on a real world dataset. For instructions on creating and accessing Jupyter notebook instances that you can use to run the example in SageMaker AI, see cite15†Amazon SageMaker notebook instances .
L105: After creating and opening a notebook instance, choose the SageMaker AI Examples tab to see a list of all of the SageMaker AI examples. To open a notebook, choose its Use tab, and choose Create copy.
L106: For more information about the Amazon SageMaker AI DeepAR algorithm, see the following blog posts:
L107: 
L108:   * cite16†Now available in Amazon SageMaker AI: DeepAR algorithm for more accurate time series forecasting†aws.amazon.com L109: 
L110:   * cite17†Deep demand forecasting with Amazon SageMaker AI†aws.amazon.com L111:

L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Streaming ETL jobs in AWS Glue - AWS Glue
L3: 
L4: cite1†Creating a connection for a Kafka data stream cite2†Creating a Data Catalog table for a streaming source cite3†Notes and restrictions for Avro streaming sources cite4†Applying grok patterns to streaming sources cite5†Defining job properties for a streaming ETL job cite6†Streaming ETL notes and restrictions L5: # Streaming ETL jobs in AWS Glue
L6: 
L7: You can create streaming extract, transform, and load (ETL) jobs that run continuously, consume data from streaming sources like Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Apache Kafka, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK). The jobs cleanse and transform the data, and then load the results into Amazon S3 data lakes or JDBC data stores.
L8: Additionally, you can produce data for Amazon Kinesis Data Streams streams. This feature is only available when writing AWS Glue scripts. For more information, see cite7†Kinesis connections .
L9: By default, AWS Glue processes and writes out data in 100-second windows. This allows data to be processed efficiently and permits aggregations to be performed on data arriving later than expected. You can modify this window size to increase timeliness or aggregation accuracy. AWS Glue streaming jobs use checkpoints rather than job bookmarks to track the data that has been read.
L10: ###### Note
L11: 
L12: AWS Glue bills hourly for streaming ETL jobs while they are running.
L13: 
L14: This video discusses streaming ETL cost challenges, and cost-saving features in AWS Glue.
L15: 
L16: cite8†iframe†www.youtube-nocookie.com L17: 
L18: Creating a streaming ETL job involves the following steps:
L19: 
L20:   1. For an Apache Kafka streaming source, create an AWS Glue connection to the Kafka source or the Amazon MSK cluster.
L21: 
L22:   2. Manually create a Data Catalog table for the streaming source.
L23:   3. Create an ETL job for the streaming data source. Define streaming-specific job properties, and supply your own script or optionally modify the generated script.
L24: 
L25: For more information, see cite9†Streaming ETL in AWS Glue .
L26: When creating a streaming ETL job for Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, you don't have to create an AWS Glue connection. However, if there is a connection attached to the AWS Glue streaming ETL job that has Kinesis Data Streams as a source, then a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint to Kinesis is required. For more information, see cite10†Creating an interface endpoint in the Amazon VPC User Guide.
L27: When specifying a Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream in another account, you must setup the roles and policies to allow cross-account access. For more information, see cite11†Example: Read From a Kinesis Stream in a Different Account .
L28: AWS Glue streaming ETL jobs can auto-detect compressed data, transparently decompress the streaming data, perform the usual transformations on the input source, and load to the output store.
L29: 
L30: AWS Glue supports auto-decompression for the following compression types given the input format:
L31: Compression type  | Avro file  | Avro datum  | JSON  | CSV  | Grok
L32: --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
L33: BZIP2  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes
L34: GZIP  | No  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes
L35: SNAPPY  | Yes (raw Snappy)  | Yes (framed Snappy)  | Yes (framed Snappy)  | Yes (framed Snappy)  | Yes (framed Snappy)
L36: XZ  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes
L37: ZSTD  | Yes  | No  | No  | No  | No
L38: DEFLATE  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes  | Yes
L39: ###### Topics
L40: 
L41:   * cite1†Creating an AWS Glue connection for an Apache Kafka data stream L42: 
L43:   * cite2†Creating a Data Catalog table for a streaming source L44: 
L45:   * cite3†Notes and restrictions for Avro streaming sources L46: 
L47:   * cite4†Applying grok patterns to streaming sources L48: 
L49:   * cite5†Defining job properties for a streaming ETL job L50: 
L51:   * cite6†Streaming ETL notes and restrictions L52: 
L53: ## Creating an AWS Glue connection for an Apache Kafka data stream
L54: 
L55: To read from an Apache Kafka stream, you must create an AWS Glue connection.
L56: ###### To create an AWS Glue connection for a Kafka source (Console)
L57: 
L58:   1. Open the AWS Glue console at cite12†https://console.aws.amazon.com/glue/†console.aws.amazon.com .
L59: 
L60:   2. In the navigation pane, under Data catalog, choose Connections.
L61: 
L62:   3. Choose Add connection, and on the Set up your connection’s properties page, enter a connection name.
L63: ###### Note
L64: 
L65: For more information about specifying connection properties, see cite13†AWS Glue connection properties. .
L66: 
L67:   4. For Connection type, choose Kafka.
L68: 
L69:   5. For Kafka bootstrap servers URLs, enter the host and port number for the bootstrap brokers for your Amazon MSK cluster or Apache Kafka cluster. Use only Transport Layer Security (TLS) endpoints for establishing the initial connection to the Kafka cluster. Plaintext endpoints are not supported.
L70: The following is an example list of hostname and port number pairs for an Amazon MSK cluster.
L71: 
L72:     `myserver1.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9094,myserver2.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9094,
L73:     myserver3.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9094`
L74: 
L75: For more information about getting the bootstrap broker information, see cite14†Getting the Bootstrap Brokers for an Amazon MSK Cluster in the Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka Developer Guide.
L76:   6. If you want a secure connection to the Kafka data source, select Require SSL connection, and for Kafka private CA certificate location, enter a valid Amazon S3 path to a custom SSL certificate.
L77: 
L78: For an SSL connection to self-managed Kafka, the custom certificate is mandatory. It's optional for Amazon MSK.
L79: 
L80: For more information about specifying a custom certificate for Kafka, see cite15†AWS Glue SSL connection properties .
L81:   7. Use AWS Glue Studio or the AWS CLI to specify a Kafka client authentication method. To access AWS Glue Studio select AWS Glue from the ETL menu in the left navigation pane.
L82: 
L83: For more information about Kafka client authentication methods, see cite16†AWS Glue Kafka connection properties for client authentication .
L84: 
L85:   8. Optionally enter a description, and then choose Next.
L86:   9. For an Amazon MSK cluster, specify its virtual private cloud (VPC), subnet, and security group. The VPC information is optional for self-managed Kafka.
L87: 
L88:   10. Choose Next to review all connection properties, and then choose Finish.
L89: 
L90: For more information about AWS Glue connections, see cite17†Connecting to data .
L91: ### AWS Glue Kafka connection properties for client authentication
L92: 
L93: SASL/GSSAPI (Kerberos) authentication
L94: 
L95: 
L96: Choosing this authentication method will allow you to specify Kerberos properties.
L97: 
L98: Kerberos Keytab
L99: 
L100: 
L101: Choose the location of the keytab file. A keytab stores long-term keys for one or more principals. For more information, see cite18†MIT Kerberos Documentation: Keytab†web.mit.edu .
L102: 
L103: Kerberos krb5.conf file
L104: Choose the krb5.conf file. This contains the default realm (a logical network, similar to a domain, that defines a group of systems under the same KDC) and the location of the KDC server. For more information, see cite19†MIT Kerberos Documentation: krb5.conf†web.mit.edu .
L105: 
L106: Kerberos principal and Kerberos service name
L107: 
L108: 
L109: Enter the Kerberos principal and service name. For more information, see cite20†MIT Kerberos Documentation: Kerberos principal†web.mit.edu .
L110: 
L111: SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 authentication
L112: Choosing this authentication method will allow you to specify authentication credentials.
L113: 
L114: AWS Secrets Manager
L115: 
L116: 
L117: Search for your token in the Search box by typing the name or ARN.
L118: 
L119: Provider username and password directly
L120: 
L121: 
L122: Search for your token in the Search box by typing the name or ARN.
L123: 
L124: SSL client authentication
L125: Choosing this authentication method allows you to select the location of the Kafka client keystore by browsing Amazon S3. Optionally, you can enter the Kafka client keystore password and Kafka client key password.
L126: 
L127: IAM authentication
L128: 
L129: 
L130: This authentication method does not require any additional specifications and is only applicable when the Streaming source is MSK Kafka.
L131: 
L132: SASL/PLAIN authentication
L133: 
L134: 
L135: Choosing this authentication method allows you to specify authentication credentials.
L136: ## Creating a Data Catalog table for a streaming source
L137: 
L138: A Data Catalog table that specifies source data stream properties, including the data schema can be manually created for a streaming source. This table is used as the data source for the streaming ETL job.
L139: If you don't know the schema of the data in the source data stream, you can create the table without a schema. Then when you create the streaming ETL job, you can turn on the AWS Glue schema detection function. AWS Glue determines the schema from the streaming data.
L140: 
L141: Use the cite12†AWS Glue console†console.aws.amazon.com , the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or the AWS Glue API to create the table. For information about creating a table manually with the AWS Glue console, see cite21†Creating tables .
L142: ###### Note
L143: 
L144: You can't use the AWS Lake Formation console to create the table; you must use the AWS Glue console.
L145: 
L146: Also consider the following information for streaming sources in Avro format or for log data that you can apply Grok patterns to.
L147: 
L148:   * cite3†Notes and restrictions for Avro streaming sources L149: 
L150:   * cite4†Applying grok patterns to streaming sources L151: 
L152: ###### Topics
L153: 
L154:   * cite22†Kinesis data source L155: 
L156:   * cite23†Kafka data source L157: 
L158:   * cite24†AWS Glue Schema Registry table source L159: ### Kinesis data source
L160: 
L161: When creating the table, set the following streaming ETL properties (console).
L162: 
L163: Type of Source
L164: 
L165: 
L166: Kinesis
L167: 
L168: For a Kinesis source in the same account:
L169: 
L170: 
L171: Region
L172: 
L173: 
L174: The AWS Region where the Amazon Kinesis Data Streams service resides. The Region and Kinesis stream name are together translated to a Stream ARN.
L175: 
L176: Example: https://kinesis.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
L177: 
L178: Kinesis stream name
L179: Stream name as described in cite25†Creating a Stream in the Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide.
L180: 
L181: For a Kinesis source in another account, refer to cite11†this example to set up the roles and policies to allow cross-account access. Configure these settings:
L182: 
L183: 
L184: Stream ARN
L185: 
L186: 
L187: The ARN of the Kinesis data stream that the consumer is registered with. For more information, see cite26†Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) and AWS Service Namespaces in the AWS General Reference.
L188: 
L189: Assumed Role ARN
L190: The Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the role to assume.
L191: 
L192: Session name (optional)
L193: 
L194: 
L195: An identifier for the assumed role session.
L196: Use the role session name to uniquely identify a session when the same role is assumed by different principals or for different reasons. In cross-account scenarios, the role session name is visible to, and can be logged by the account that owns the role. The role session name is also used in the ARN of the assumed role principal.
L197: This means that subsequent cross-account API requests that use the temporary security credentials will expose the role session name to the external account in their AWS CloudTrail logs.
L198: ###### To set streaming ETL properties for Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (AWS Glue API or AWS CLI)
L199:   * To set up streaming ETL properties for a Kinesis source in the same account, specify the `streamName` and `endpointUrl` parameters in the `StorageDescriptor` structure of the `CreateTable` API operation or the `create_table` CLI command.
L200: 
L201:     `"StorageDescriptor": {
L202:     	"Parameters": {
L203:     		"typeOfData": "kinesis",
L204:     		"streamName": "sample-stream",
L205:     		"endpointUrl": "https://kinesis.us-east-1.amazonaws.com"
L206:     	}
L207:     	...
L208:     }
L209:     					`
L210: 
L211: Or, specify the `streamARN`.
L212: ###### Example
L213: 
L214:     `"StorageDescriptor": {
L215:     	"Parameters": {
L216:     		"typeOfData": "kinesis",
L217:     		"streamARN": "arn:aws:kinesis:us-east-1:123456789:stream/sample-stream"
L218:     	}
L219:     	...
L220:     }`
L221:   * To set up streaming ETL properties for a Kinesis source in another account, specify the `streamARN`, `awsSTSRoleARN` and `awsSTSSessionName` (optional) parameters in the `StorageDescriptor` structure in the `CreateTable` API operation or the `create_table` CLI command.
L222: 
L223:     `"StorageDescriptor": {
L224:     	"Parameters": {
L225:     		"typeOfData": "kinesis",
L226:     		"streamARN": "arn:aws:kinesis:us-east-1:123456789:stream/sample-stream",
L227:     		"awsSTSRoleARN": "arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/sample-assume-role-arn",
L228:     		"awsSTSSessionName": "optional-session"
L229:     	}
L230:     	...
L231:     }`
L232: ### Kafka data source
L233: 
L234: When creating the table, set the following streaming ETL properties (console).
L235: 
L236: Type of Source
L237: 
L238: 
L239: Kafka
L240: 
L241: For a Kafka source:
L242: 
L243: 
L244: Topic name
L245: 
L246: 
L247: Topic name as specified in Kafka.
L248: 
L249: Connection
L250: 
L251: 
L252: An AWS Glue connection that references a Kafka source, as described in cite1†Creating an AWS Glue connection for an Apache Kafka data stream .
L253: ### AWS Glue Schema Registry table source
L254: 
L255: To use AWS Glue Schema Registry for streaming jobs, follow the instructions at cite27†Use case: AWS Glue Data Catalog to create or update a Schema Registry table.
L256: 
L257: Currently, AWS Glue Streaming supports only Glue Schema Registry Avro format with schema inference set to `false`.
L258: ## Notes and restrictions for Avro streaming sources
L259: 
L260: The following notes and restrictions apply for streaming sources in the Avro format:
L261: 
L262:   * When schema detection is turned on, the Avro schema must be included in the payload. When turned off, the payload should contain only data.
L263:   * Some Avro data types are not supported in dynamic frames. You can't specify these data types when defining the schema with the Define a schema page in the create table wizard in the AWS Glue console. During schema detection, unsupported types in the Avro schema are converted to supported types as follows:
L264: 
L265:     * `EnumType => StringType`
L266: 
L267:     * `FixedType => BinaryType`
L268: 
L269:     * `UnionType => StructType`
L270:   * If you define the table schema using the Define a schema page in the console, the implied root element type for the schema is `record`. If you want a root element type other than `record`, for example `array` or `map`, you can't specify the schema using the Define a schema page. Instead you must skip that page and specify the schema either as a table property or within the ETL script.
L271:     * To specify the schema in the table properties, complete the create table wizard, edit the table details, and add a new key-value pair under Table properties. Use the key `avroSchema`, and enter a schema JSON object for the value, as shown in the following screenshot.
L272: cite28†Image: Under the Table properties heading, there are two columns of text fields. The left-hand column heading is Key, and the right-hand column heading is Value. The key/value pair in the first row is classification/avro. The key/value pair in the second row is avroSchema/{"type":"array","items":"string"}. L273:     * To specify the schema in the ETL script, modify the `datasource0` assignment statement and add the `avroSchema` key to the `additional_options` argument, as shown in the following Python and Scala examples.
L274: Python
L275: 
L276: 
L277:         `SCHEMA_STRING = ‘{"type":"array","items":"string"}’
L278:         datasource0 = glueContext.create_data_frame.from_catalog(database = "`database`", table_name = "`table_name`", transformation_ctx = "datasource0", additional_options = {"startingPosition": "TRIM_HORIZON", "inferSchema": "false", "avroSchema": SCHEMA_STRING})
L279:         `
L280: Scala
L281: 
L282: 
L283:         `val SCHEMA_STRING = """{"type":"array","items":"string"}"""
L284:         val datasource0 = glueContext.getCatalogSource(database = "`database`", tableName = "`table_name`", redshiftTmpDir = "", transformationContext = "datasource0", additionalOptions = JsonOptions(s"""{"startingPosition": "TRIM_HORIZON", "inferSchema": "false", "avroSchema":"$SCHEMA_STRING"}""")).getDataFrame()
L285:         `
L286: ## Applying grok patterns to streaming sources
L287: 
L288: You can create a streaming ETL job for a log data source and use Grok patterns to convert the logs to structured data. The ETL job then processes the data as a structured data source. You specify the Grok patterns to apply when you create the Data Catalog table for the streaming source.
L289: 
L290: For information about Grok patterns and custom pattern string values, see cite29†Writing grok custom classifiers .
L291: ###### To add grok patterns to the Data Catalog table (console)
L292: 
L293:   * Use the create table wizard, and create the table with the parameters specified in cite2†Creating a Data Catalog table for a streaming source . Specify the data format as Grok, fill in the Grok pattern field, and optionally add custom patterns under Custom patterns (optional).
L294: 
L295: cite30†Image: * L296: 
L297: Press Enter after each custom pattern.
L298: ###### To add grok patterns to the Data Catalog table (AWS Glue API or AWS CLI)
L299: 
L300:   * Add the `GrokPattern` parameter and optionally the `CustomPatterns` parameter to the `CreateTable` API operation or the `create_table` CLI command.
L301: 
L302:     ` "Parameters": {
L303:     ...
L304:         "grokPattern": "string",
L305:         "grokCustomPatterns": "string",
L306:     ...
L307:     },`
L308: 
L309: Express `grokCustomPatterns` as a string and use "\n" as the separator between patterns.
L310: 
L311: The following is an example of specifying these parameters.
L312: ###### Example
L313: 
L314:     `"parameters": {
L315:     ...
L316:         "grokPattern": "%{USERNAME:username} %{DIGIT:digit:int}",
L317:         "grokCustomPatterns": "digit \d",
L318:     ...
L319:     }
L320:     `
L321: ## Defining job properties for a streaming ETL job
L322: 
L323: When you define a streaming ETL job in the AWS Glue console, provide the following streams-specific properties. For descriptions of additional job properties, see cite31†Defining job properties for Spark jobs .
L324: 
L325: IAM role
L326: 
L327: 
L328: Specify the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that is used for authorization to resources that are used to run the job, access streaming sources, and access target data stores.
L329: For access to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, attach the `AmazonKinesisFullAccess` AWS managed policy to the role, or attach a similar IAM policy that permits more fine-grained access. For sample policies, see cite32†Controlling Access to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Resources Using IAM .
L330: 
L331: For more information about permissions for running jobs in AWS Glue, see cite33†Identity and access management for AWS Glue .
L332: 
L333: Type
L334: 
L335: 
L336: Choose Spark streaming.
L337: 
L338: AWS Glue version
L339: The AWS Glue version determines the versions of Apache Spark, and Python or Scala, that are available to the job. Choose a selection that specifies the version of Python or Scala available to the job. AWS Glue Version 2.0 with Python 3 support is the default for streaming ETL jobs.
L340: 
L341: Maintenance window
L342: 
L343: 
L344: Specifies a window where a streaming job can be restarted. See cite34†Maintenance windows for AWS Glue Streaming .
L345: 
L346: Job timeout
L347: 
L348: 
L349: Optionally enter a duration in minutes. The default value is blank.
L350:   * Streaming jobs must have a timeout value less than 7 days or 10080 minutes.
L351: 
L352:   * When the value is left blank, the job will be restarted after 7 days, if you have not set up a maintenance window. If you have set up a maintenance window, the job will be restarted during the maintenance window after 7 days.
L353: 
L354: Data source
L355: 
L356: 
L357: Specify the table that you created in cite2†Creating a Data Catalog table for a streaming source .
L358: 
L359: Data target
L360: 
L361: 
L362: Do one of the following:
L363:   * Choose Create tables in your data target and specify the following data target properties.
L364: 
L365: Data store
L366: 
L367: 
L368: Choose Amazon S3 or JDBC.
L369: 
L370: Format
L371: 
L372: 
L373: Choose any format. All are supported for streaming.
L374: 
L375:   * Choose Use tables in the data catalog and update your data target, and choose a table for a JDBC data store.
L376: 
L377: Output schema definition
L378: 
L379: 
L380: Do one of the following:
L381:   * Choose Automatically detect schema of each record to turn on schema detection. AWS Glue determines the schema from the streaming data.
L382: 
L383:   * Choose Specify output schema for all records to use the Apply Mapping transform to define the output schema.
L384: 
L385: Script
L386: Optionally supply your own script or modify the generated script to perform operations that the Apache Spark Structured Streaming engine supports. For information on the available operations, see cite35†Operations on streaming DataFrames/Datasets†spark.apache.org .
L387: ## Streaming ETL notes and restrictions
L388: 
L389: Keep in mind the following notes and restrictions:
L390: 
L391:   * Auto-decompression for AWS Glue streaming ETL jobs is only available for the supported compression types. Also note the following:
L392: 
L393:     * Framed Snappy refers to the official cite36†framing format†github.com for Snappy.
L394: 
L395:     * Deflate is supported in Glue version 3.0, not Glue version 2.0.
L396: 
L397:   * When using schema detection, you cannot perform joins of streaming data.
L398:   * AWS Glue streaming ETL jobs do not support the Union data type for AWS Glue Schema Registry with Avro format.
L399: 
L400:   * Your ETL script can use AWS Glue's built-in transforms and the transforms native to Apache Spark Structured Streaming. For more information, see cite35†Operations on streaming DataFrames/Datasets†spark.apache.org on the Apache Spark website or cite37†AWS Glue PySpark transforms reference .
L401:   * AWS Glue streaming ETL jobs use checkpoints to keep track of the data that has been read. Therefore, a stopped and restarted job picks up where it left off in the stream. If you want to reprocess data, you can delete the checkpoint folder referenced in the script.
L402: 
L403:   * Job bookmarks aren't supported.
L404: 
L405:   * To use enhanced fan-out feature of Kinesis Data Streams in your job, consult cite38†Using enhanced fan-out in Kinesis streaming jobs .
L406:   * If you use a Data Catalog table created from AWS Glue Schema Registry, when a new schema version becomes available, to reflect the new schema, you need to do the following:
L407: 
L408:     1. Stop the jobs associated with the table.
L409: 
L410:     2. Update the schema for the Data Catalog table.
L411: 
L412:     3. Restart the jobs associated with the table.

L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Logging Amazon SageMaker AI API calls using AWS CloudTrail - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Amazon SageMaker AI data events in CloudTrail cite2†Amazon SageMaker AI management events in CloudTrail cite3†Operations Performed by Automatic Model Tuning cite4†Amazon SageMaker AI event examples L5: # Logging Amazon SageMaker AI API calls using AWS CloudTrail
L6: Amazon SageMaker AI is integrated with cite5†AWS CloudTrail , a service that provides a record of actions taken by a user, role, or an AWS service. CloudTrail captures all API calls for Amazon SageMaker AI as events. The calls captured include calls from the Amazon SageMaker AI console and code calls to the Amazon SageMaker AI API operations.
L7: Using the information collected by CloudTrail, you can determine the request that was made to Amazon SageMaker AI, the IP address from which the request was made, when it was made, and additional details.
L8: Every event or log entry contains information about who generated the request. The identity information helps you determine the following:
L9: 
L10:   * Whether the request was made with root user or user credentials.
L11: 
L12:   * Whether the request was made on behalf of an IAM Identity Center user.
L13: 
L14:   * Whether the request was made with temporary security credentials for a role or federated user.
L15: 
L16:   * Whether the request was made by another AWS service.
L17: CloudTrail is active in your AWS account when you create the account and you automatically have access to the CloudTrail Event history. The CloudTrail Event history provides a viewable, searchable, downloadable, and immutable record of the past 90 days of recorded management events in an AWS Region. For more information, see cite6†Working with CloudTrail Event history in the AWS CloudTrail User Guide. There are no CloudTrail charges for viewing the Event history.
L18: For an ongoing record of events in your AWS account past 90 days, create a trail or a cite7†CloudTrail Lake event data store.
L19: 
L20: CloudTrail trails
L21: A trail enables CloudTrail to deliver log files to an Amazon S3 bucket. All trails created using the AWS Management Console are multi-Region. You can create a single-Region or a multi-Region trail by using the AWS CLI. Creating a multi-Region trail is recommended because you capture activity in all AWS Regions in your account. If you create a single-Region trail, you can view only the events logged in the trail's AWS Region.
L22: For more information about trails, see cite8†Creating a trail for your AWS account and cite9†Creating a trail for an organization in the AWS CloudTrail User Guide.
L23: You can deliver one copy of your ongoing management events to your Amazon S3 bucket at no charge from CloudTrail by creating a trail, however, there are Amazon S3 storage charges. For more information about CloudTrail pricing, see cite10†AWS CloudTrail Pricing†aws.amazon.com . For information about Amazon S3 pricing, see cite11†Amazon S3 Pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L24: 
L25: CloudTrail Lake event data stores
L26: CloudTrail Lake lets you run SQL-based queries on your events. CloudTrail Lake converts existing events in row-based JSON format to cite12†Apache ORC†orc.apache.org format. ORC is a columnar storage format that is optimized for fast retrieval of data. Events are aggregated into event data stores, which are immutable collections of events based on criteria that you select by applying cite13†advanced event selectors .
L27: The selectors that you apply to an event data store control which events persist and are available for you to query. For more information about CloudTrail Lake, see cite7†Working with AWS CloudTrail Lake in the AWS CloudTrail User Guide.
L28: CloudTrail Lake event data stores and queries incur costs. When you create an event data store, you choose the cite14†pricing option you want to use for the event data store. The pricing option determines the cost for ingesting and storing events, and the default and maximum retention period for the event data store. For more information about CloudTrail pricing, see cite10†AWS CloudTrail Pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L29: For security purposes, you can monitor CloudTrail logs to identify abnormal user activity. For more information about monitoring logs, see cite15†Logging and Monitoring .
L30: ## Amazon SageMaker AI data events in CloudTrail
L31: 
L32: cite16†Data events provide information about the resource operations performed on or in a resource (for example, reading or writing to an Amazon S3 object). These are also known as data plane operations. Data events are often high-volume activities. By default, CloudTrail doesn’t log data events. The CloudTrail Event history doesn't record data events.
L33: Additional charges apply for data events. For more information about CloudTrail pricing, see cite10†AWS CloudTrail Pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L34: 
L35: You can log data events for various Amazon SageMaker AI resource types by using the CloudTrail console, AWS CLI, or CloudTrail API operations. For more information about how to log data events, see cite17†Logging data events with the AWS Management Console and cite18†Logging data events with the AWS Command Line Interface in the AWS CloudTrail User Guide.
L36: The following table lists the Amazon SageMaker AI resource types for which you can log data events. The Resource type (console) column shows the value to choose from the Resource type list on the CloudTrail console. The resources.type value column shows the `resources.type` value, which you would specify when configuring advanced event selectors using the AWS CLI or CloudTrail APIs. The Data APIs logged to CloudTrail column shows the API calls logged to CloudTrail for the resource type.
L37: Resource type (console)  | resources.type value  | Data APIs logged to CloudTrail
L38: --- | --- | ---
L39: SageMaker endpoint  | `AWS::SageMaker::Endpoint`  |
L40: 
L41:   * cite19†InvokeEndpoint L42:   * cite20†InvokeEndpointAsync L43:   * cite21†InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream L44: SageMaker jobs  | `AWS::SageMaker::Job`  |
L45: 
L46:   * cite22†CompleteRollout L47:   * cite23†Sample L48:   * cite24†SampleWithResponseStream L49: ###### Note
L50: 
L51: The `InvokeEndpoint`, `InvokeEndpointAsync`, `Sample`, and `SampleWithResponseStream` API calls don't log the request parameters.
L52: 
L53: You can configure advanced event selectors to filter on the `eventName`, `readOnly`, and `resources.ARN` fields to log only those events that are important to you. For more information about these fields, see cite25†AdvancedFieldSelector in the AWS CloudTrail API Reference.
L54: The following example shows you how to log data events for an Amazon SageMaker endpoint and an Amazon SageMaker job. In this example, you use the cite26†put-event-selectors AWS CLI command to add advanced event selectors that capture data events from your endpoint. You should have an existing CloudTrail trail. Before running the command, you can also save the advanced event selectors JSON object in a file like the following:
L55: 
L56:     `[
L57:       {
L58:         "FieldSelectors": [
L59:           {
L60:             "Field": "eventCategory",
L61:             "Equals": ["Data"]
L62:           },
L63:           {
L64:             "Field": "resources.ARN",
L65:             "Equals": ["arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-1:111122223333:endpoint/`your-inference-endpoint-arn`"]
L66:           },
L67:           {
L68:             "Field": "resources.type",
L69:             "Equals": ["AWS::SageMaker::Endpoint"]
L70:           }
L71:         ]
L72:       },
L73:       {
L74:         "FieldSelectors": [
L75:           {
L76:             "Field": "eventCategory",
L77:             "Equals": ["Data"]
L78:           },
L79:           {
L80:             "Field": "resources.ARN",
L81:             "Equals": ["arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-1:111122223333:job/`your-job-arn`"]
L82:           },
L83:           {
L84:             "Field": "resources.type",
L85:             "Equals": ["AWS::SageMaker::Job"]
L86:           }
L87:         ]
L88:       }
L89:     ]`
L90: Then, you can run the following command to start logging data events from the endpoint.
L91: 
L92:     `aws cloudtrail put-event-selectors
L93:           --trail-name `your-trail-name`
L94:           --advanced-event-selectors=file://`advanced-event-selectors.json` # specify your previously created JSON file`
L95: ## Amazon SageMaker AI management events in CloudTrail
L96: 
L97: cite27†Management events provide information about management operations that are performed on resources in your AWS account. These are also known as control plane operations. By default, CloudTrail logs management events.
L98: Amazon SageMaker AI logs all Amazon SageMaker AI control plane operations as management events. For a list of the Amazon SageMaker AI control plane operations that Amazon SageMaker AI logs to CloudTrail, see the cite28†Amazon SageMaker AI API Reference .
L99: ## Operations Performed by Automatic Model Tuning
L100: SageMaker AI supports logging non-API service events to your CloudTrail log files for automatic model tuning jobs. These events are related to your tuning jobs but, are not the direct result of a customer request to the public AWS API. For example, when you create a hyperparameter tuning job by calling cite29†`CreateHyperParameterTuningJob` , SageMaker AI creates training jobs to evaluate various combinations of hyperparameters to find the best result.
L101: Similarly, when you call cite30†`StopHyperParameterTuningJob` to stop a hyperparameter tuning job, SageMaker AI might stop any of the associated running training jobs. Non-API events for your tuning jobs are logged to CloudTrail to help you improve governance, compliance, and operational and risk auditing of your AWS account.
L102: Log entries that result from non-API service events have an `eventType` of `AwsServiceEvent` instead of `AwsApiCall`.
L103: ## Amazon SageMaker AI event examples
L104: 
L105: An event represents a single request from any source and includes information about the requested API operation, the date and time of the operation, request parameters, and so on. CloudTrail log files aren't an ordered stack trace of the public API calls, so events don't appear in any specific order.
L106: The following example shows a CloudTrail event that demonstrates the `CreateEndpoint` operation.

L109:         "eventVersion":"1.05",
L110:         "userIdentity": {
L111:             "type":"IAMUser",
L112:             "principalId":"AIXDAYQEXAMPLEUMLYNGL",
L113:             "arn":"arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/intern",
L114:             "accountId":"123456789012",
L115:             "accessKeyId":"ASXIAGXEXAMPLEQULKNXV",
L116:             "userName":"intern"
L117:         },
L118:         "eventTime":"2018-01-02T13:39:06Z",
L119:         "eventSource":"sagemaker.amazonaws.com",
L120:         "eventName":"CreateEndpoint",
L121:         "awsRegion":"us-west-2",
L122:         "sourceIPAddress":"127.0.0.1",
L123:         "userAgent":"USER_AGENT",
L124:         "requestParameters": {
L125:             "endpointName":"ExampleEndpoint",
L126:             "endpointConfigName":"ExampleEndpointConfig"
L127:         },
L128:         "responseElements": {
L129:             "endpointArn":"arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:123456789012:endpoint/exampleendpoint"
L130:         },
L131:         "requestID":"6b1b42b9-EXAMPLE",
L132:         "eventID":"a6f85b21-EXAMPLE",
L133:         "eventType":"AwsApiCall",
L134:         "recipientAccountId":"444455556666"
L135:     }`
L136: The following example shows a CloudTrail event that demonstrates the `CreateModel` operation.
L137: 
L138:     `{
L139:         "eventVersion":"1.05",
L140:         "userIdentity": {
L141:             "type":"IAMUser",
L142:             "principalId":"AIXDAYQEXAMPLEUMLYNGL",
L143:             "arn":"arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/intern",
L144:             "accountId":"123456789012",
L145:             "accessKeyId":"ASXIAGXEXAMPLEQULKNXV",
L146:             "userName":"intern"
L147:         },
L148:         "eventTime":"2018-01-02T15:23:46Z",
L149:         "eventSource":"sagemaker.amazonaws.com",
L150:         "eventName":"CreateModel",
L151:         "awsRegion":"us-west-2",
L152:         "sourceIPAddress":"127.0.0.1",
L153:         "userAgent":"USER_AGENT",
