Binary Model Insights - Amazon Machine Learning (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/machine-learning/latest/dg/binary-model-insights.html)
citeturn13view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 2 days ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/machine-learning/latest/dg/binary-model-insights.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 98
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Binary Model Insights - Amazon Machine Learning
L3: 
L4: cite1†Interpreting the Predictions L5: 
L6: # Binary Model Insights
L7: ## Interpreting the Predictions
L8: The actual output of many binary classification algorithms is a prediction score. The score indicates the system's certainty that the given observation belongs to the positive class (the actual target value is 1). Binary classification models in Amazon ML output a score that ranges from 0 to 1.
L9: As a consumer of this score, to make the decision about whether the observation should be classified as 1 or 0, you interpret the score by picking a classification threshold, or cut-off, and compare the score against it. Any observations with scores higher than the cut-off are predicted as target= 1, and scores lower than the cut-off are predicted as target= 0.
L10: In Amazon ML, the default score cut-off is 0.5. You can choose to update this cut-off to match your business needs. You can use the visualizations in the console to understand how the choice of cut-off will affect your application.
L11: ### Measuring ML Model Accuracy
L12: 
L13: Amazon ML provides an industry-standard accuracy metric for binary classification models called Area Under the (Receiver Operating Characteristic) Curve (AUC). AUC measures the ability of the model to predict a higher score for positive examples as compared to negative examples. Because it is independent of the score cut-off, you can get a sense of the prediction accuracy of your model from the AUC metric without picking a threshold.
L14: The AUC metric returns a decimal value from 0 to 1. AUC values near 1 indicate an ML model that is highly accurate. Values near 0.5 indicate an ML model that is no better than guessing at random. Values near 0 are unusual to see, and typically indicate a problem with the data. Essentially, an AUC near 0 says that the ML model has learned the correct patterns, but is using them to make predictions that are flipped from reality ('0's are predicted as '1's and vice versa).
L15: For more information about AUC, go to the cite2†Receiver operating characteristic†en.wikipedia.org page on Wikipedia.
L16: The baseline AUC metric for a binary model is 0.5. It is the value for a hypothetical ML model that randomly predicts a 1 or 0 answer. Your binary ML model should perform better than this value to begin to be valuable.
L17: ### Using the Performance Visualization
L18: 
L19: To explore the accuracy of the ML model, you can review the graphs on the Evaluation page on the Amazon ML console. This page shows you two histograms: a) a histogram of the scores for the actual positives (the target is 1) and b) a histogram of scores for the actual negatives (the target is 0) in the evaluation data.
L20: An ML model that has good predictive accuracy will predict higher scores to the actual 1s and lower scores to the actual 0s. A perfect model will have the two histograms at two different ends of the x-axis showing that actual positives all got high scores and actual negatives all got low scores. However, ML models make mistakes, and a typical graph will show that the two histograms overlap at certain scores.
L21: An extremely poor performing model will be unable to distinguish between the positive and negative classes, and both classes will have mostly overlapping histograms.
L22: cite3†Image: image49 L23: 
L24: Using the visualizations, you can identify the number of predictions that fall into the two types of correct predictions and the two types of incorrect predictions.
L25: 
L26: Correct Predictions
L27: 
L28:   * True positive (TP): Amazon ML predicted the value as 1, and the true value is 1.
L29: 
L30:   * True negative (TN): Amazon ML predicted the value as 0, and the true value is 0.
L31: 
L32: Erroneous Predictions
L33: 
L34:   * False positive (FP): Amazon ML predicted the value as 1, but the true value is 0.
L35:   * False negative (FN): Amazon ML predicted the value as 0, but the true value is 1.
L36: ###### Note
L37: 
L38: The number of TP, TN, FP, and FN depends on the selected score threshold, and optimizing for any of one of these numbers would mean making a tradeoff on the others. A high number of TPs typically results in a high number of FPs and a low number of TNs.
L39: ### Adjusting the Score Cut-off
L40: 
L41: ML models work by generating numeric prediction scores, and then applying a cut-off to convert these scores into binary 0/1 labels. By changing the score cut-off, you can adjust the model's behavior when it makes a mistake. On the Evaluation page in the Amazon ML console, you can review the impact of various score cut-offs, and you can save the score cut-off that you would like to use for your model.
L42: When you adjust the score cut-off threshold, observe the trade-off between the two types of errors. Moving the cut-off to the left captures more true positives, but the trade-off is an increase in the number of false positive errors. Moving it to the right captures less of the false positive errors, but the trade-off is that it will miss some true positives. For your predictive application, you make the decision which kind of error is more tolerable by selecting an appropriate cut-off score.
L43: ### Reviewing Advanced Metrics
L44: 
L45: Amazon ML provides the following additional metrics to measure the predictive accuracy of the ML model: accuracy, precision, recall, and false positive rate.
L46: 
L47: #### Accuracy
L48: 
L49: Accuracy (ACC) measures the fraction of correct predictions. The range is 0 to 1. A larger value indicates better predictive accuracy:
L50: 
L51: cite4†Image: image50 L52: #### Precision
L53: 
L54: Precision measures the fraction of actual positives among those examples that are predicted as positive. The range is 0 to 1. A larger value indicates better predictive accuracy:
L55: 
L56: cite5†Image: image51 L57: 
L58: #### Recall
L59: 
L60: Recall measures the fraction of actual positives that are predicted as positive. The range is 0 to 1. A larger value indicates better predictive accuracy:
L61: 
L62: cite6†Image: image52 L63: #### False Positive Rate
L64: 
L65: The false positive rate (FPR) measures the false alarm rate or the fraction of actual negatives that are predicted as positive. The range is 0 to 1. A smaller value indicates better predictive accuracy:
L66: 
L67: cite7†Image: image53 L68: 
L69: Depending on your business problem, you might be more interested in a model that performs well for a specific subset of these metrics. For example, two business applications might have very different requirements for their ML model:
L70:   * One application might need to be extremely sure about the positive predictions actually being positive (high precision), and be able to afford to misclassify some positive examples as negative (moderate recall).
L71: 
L72:   * Another application might need to correctly predict as many positive examples as possible (high recall), and will accept some negative examples being misclassified as positive (moderate precision).
L73: Amazon ML allows you to choose a score cut-off that corresponds to a particular value of any of the preceding advanced metrics. It also shows the tradeoffs incurred with optimizing for any one metric. For example, if you select a cut-off that corresponds to a high precision, you typically will have to trade that off with a lower recall.
L74: ###### Note
L75: 
L76: You have to save the score cut-off for it to take effect on classifying any future predictions by your ML model.

L2: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) Algorithm - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Input/Output Interface for the PCA Algorithm cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the PCA Algorithm cite3†Sample Notebooks L5: # Principal Component Analysis (PCA) Algorithm
L6: PCA is an unsupervised machine learning algorithm that attempts to reduce the dimensionality (number of features) within a dataset while still retaining as much information as possible. This is done by finding a new set of features called components, which are composites of the original features that are uncorrelated with one another. They are also constrained so that the first component accounts for the largest possible variability in the data, the second component the second most variability, and so on.
L7: In Amazon SageMaker AI, PCA operates in two modes, depending on the scenario:
L8: 
L9:   * regular: For datasets with sparse data and a moderate number of observations and features.
L10: 
L11:   * randomized: For datasets with both a large number of observations and features. This mode uses an approximation algorithm.
L12: 
L13: PCA uses tabular data.
L14: The rows represent observations you want to embed in a lower dimensional space. The columns represent features that you want to find a reduced approximation for. The algorithm calculates the covariance matrix (or an approximation thereof in a distributed manner), and then performs the singular value decomposition on this summary to produce the principal components.
L15: ###### Topics
L16: 
L17:   * cite1†Input/Output Interface for the PCA Algorithm L18: 
L19:   * cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the PCA Algorithm L20:

L27:   * cite6†PCA Response Formats L28: ## Input/Output Interface for the PCA Algorithm
L29: 
L30: For training, PCA expects data provided in the train channel, and optionally supports a dataset passed to the test dataset, which is scored by the final algorithm. Both `recordIO-wrapped-protobuf` and `CSV` formats are supported for training. You can use either File mode or Pipe mode to train models on data that is formatted as `recordIO-wrapped-protobuf` or as `CSV`.
L31: For inference, PCA supports `text/csv`, `application/json`, and `application/x-recordio-protobuf`. Results are returned in either `application/json` or `application/x-recordio-protobuf` format with a vector of "projections."
L32: 
L33: For more information on input and output file formats, see cite6†PCA Response Formats for inference and the cite3†PCA Sample Notebooks .
L34: ## EC2 Instance Recommendation for the PCA Algorithm
L35: 
L36: PCA supports CPU and GPU instances for training and inference. Which instance type is most performant depends heavily on the specifics of the input data. For GPU instances, PCA supports P2, P3, G4dn, and G5.
L37: ## PCA Sample Notebooks
L38: For a sample notebook that shows how to use the SageMaker AI Principal Component Analysis algorithm to analyze the images of handwritten digits from zero to nine in the MNIST dataset, see cite7†An Introduction to PCA with MNIST†sagemaker-examples.readthedocs.io . For instructions how to create and access Jupyter notebook instances that you can use to run the example in SageMaker AI, see cite8†Amazon SageMaker notebook instances .
L39: Once you have created a notebook instance and opened it, select the SageMaker AI Examples tab to see a list of all the SageMaker AI samples. The topic modeling example notebooks using the NTM algorithms are located in the Introduction to Amazon algorithms section. To open a notebook, click on its Use tab and select Create copy.

K-Means Algorithm - Amazon SageMaker AI (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/k-means.html)
citeturn16view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/k-means.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 59
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: K-Means Algorithm - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Input/Output Interface for the K-Means Algorithm cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the K-Means Algorithm cite3†Sample Notebooks L5: # K-Means Algorithm
L6: 
L7: K-means is an unsupervised learning algorithm. It attempts to find discrete groupings within data, where members of a group are as similar as possible to one another and as different as possible from members of other groups. You define the attributes that you want the algorithm to use to determine similarity.
L8: Amazon SageMaker AI uses a modified version of the web-scale k-means clustering algorithm. Compared with the original version of the algorithm, the version used by Amazon SageMaker AI is more accurate. Like the original algorithm, it scales to massive datasets and delivers improvements in training time. To do this, the version used by Amazon SageMaker AI streams mini-batches (small, random subsets) of the training data.
L9: For more information about mini-batch k-means, see cite4†Web-scale k-means Clustering†dl.acm.org .
L10: The k-means algorithm expects tabular data, where rows represent the observations that you want to cluster, and the columns represent attributes of the observations. The n attributes in each row represent a point in n-dimensional space. The Euclidean distance between these points represents the similarity of the corresponding observations. The algorithm groups observations with similar attribute values (the points corresponding to these observations are closer together).
L11: For more information about how k-means works in Amazon SageMaker AI, see cite5†How K-Means Clustering Works .
L12: ###### Topics
L13: 
L14:   * cite1†Input/Output Interface for the K-Means Algorithm L15: 
L16:   * cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the K-Means Algorithm L17: 
L18:   * cite3†K-Means Sample Notebooks L19: 
L20:   * cite5†How K-Means Clustering Works L21: 
L22:   * cite6†K-Means Hyperparameters L23: 
L24:   * cite7†Tune a K-Means Model L25: 
L26:   * cite8†K-Means Response Formats L27: ## Input/Output Interface for the K-Means Algorithm
L28: 
L29: For training, the k-means algorithm expects data to be provided in the train channel (recommended `S3DataDistributionType=ShardedByS3Key`), with an optional test channel (recommended `S3DataDistributionType=FullyReplicated`) to score the data on. Both `recordIO-wrapped-protobuf` and `CSV` formats are supported for training. You can use either File mode or Pipe mode to train models on data that is formatted as `recordIO-wrapped-protobuf` or as `CSV`.
L30: For inference, `text/csv`, `application/json`, and `application/x-recordio-protobuf` are supported. k-means returns a `closest_cluster` label and the `distance_to_cluster` for each observation.
L31: 
L32: For more information on input and output file formats, see cite8†K-Means Response Formats for inference and the cite3†K-Means Sample Notebooks . The k-means algorithm does not support multiple instance learning, in which the training set consists of labeled “bags”, each of which is a collection of unlabeled instances.
L33: ## EC2 Instance Recommendation for the K-Means Algorithm
L34: 
L35: We recommend training k-means on CPU instances. You can train on GPU instances, but should limit GPU training to single-GPU instances (such as ml.g4dn.xlarge) because only one GPU is used per instance. The k-means algorithm supports P2, P3, G4dn, and G5 instances for training and inference.
L36: ## K-Means Sample Notebooks
L37: For a sample notebook that uses the SageMaker AI K-means algorithm to segment the population of counties in the United States by attributes identified using principle component analysis, see cite9†Analyze US census data for population segmentation using Amazon SageMaker AI†sagemaker-examples.readthedocs.io . For instructions how to create and access Jupyter notebook instances that you can use to run the example in SageMaker AI, see cite10†Amazon SageMaker notebook instances .
L38: Once you have created a notebook instance and opened it, select the SageMaker AI Examples tab to see a list of all the SageMaker AI samples. To open a notebook, click on its Use tab and select Create copy.

L6: # Start an AWS Glue job with Step Functions
L7: 
L8: Learn to use Step Functions to start a job run on AWS Glue. This page lists the supported API actions and provides an example `Task` state to start a AWS Glue job.
L9: 
L10: To learn about integrating with AWS services in Step Functions, see cite3†Integrating services and cite4†Passing parameters to a service API in Step Functions .
L11: ###### Key features of Optimized AWS Glue integration
L12: 
L13:   * The cite5†Run a Job (.sync) integration pattern is available.
L14: 
L15:   * The `JobName` field is extracted from the request and inserted into the response, which normally only contains `JobRunID`.
L16: The following includes a `Task` state that starts an AWS Glue job.
L17: 
L18:     `"Glue StartJobRun": {
L19:           "Type": "Task",
L20:           "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::glue:startJobRun.sync",
L21:           "Arguments": {
L22:             "JobName": "GlueJob-JTrRO5l98qMG"
L23:           },
L24:           "Next": "ValidateOutput"
L25:         },
L26:     `
L27: ###### Parameters in Step Functions are expressed in PascalCase
L28: 
L29: Even if the native service API is in camelCase, for example the API action `startSyncExecution`, you specify parameters in PascalCase, such as: `StateMachineArn`.

citeturn19view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 2 weeks ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emr/latest/ManagementGuide/emr-plan-instances-guidelines.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 171
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Configuring Amazon EMR cluster instance types and best practices for Spot instances - Amazon EMR
L3: 
L4: cite1†What instance type should you use? cite2†When should you use Spot Instances? cite3†Calculating the required HDFS capacity of a cluster L5: # Configuring Amazon EMR cluster instance types and best practices for Spot instances
L6: 
L7: Use the guidance in this section to help you determine the instance types, purchasing options, and amount of storage to provision for each node type in an EMR cluster.
L8: ## What instance type should you use?
L9: 
L10: There are several ways to add Amazon EC2 instances to a cluster. The method you should choose depends on whether you use the instance groups configuration or the instance fleets configuration for the cluster.
L11: 
L12:   * Instance Groups
L13: 
L14:     * Manually add instances of the same type to existing core and task instance groups.
L15: 
L16:     * Manually add a task instance group, which can use a different instance type.
L17:     * Set up automatic scaling in Amazon EMR for an instance group, adding and removing instances automatically based on the value of an Amazon CloudWatch metric that you specify. For more information, see cite4†Use Amazon EMR cluster scaling to adjust for changing workloads .
L18: 
L19:   * Instance Fleets
L20: 
L21:     * Add a single task instance fleet.
L22:     * Change the target capacity for On-Demand and Spot Instances for existing core and task instance fleets. For more information, see cite5†Planning and configuring instance fleets for your Amazon EMR cluster .
L23: One way to plan the instances of your cluster is to run a test cluster with a representative sample set of data and monitor the utilization of the nodes in the cluster. For more information, see cite6†View and monitor an Amazon EMR cluster as it performs work . Another way is to calculate the capacity of the instances you are considering and compare that value against the size of your data.
L24: In general, the primary node type, which assigns tasks, doesn't require an EC2 instance with much processing power; Amazon EC2 instances for the core node type, which process tasks and store data in HDFS, need both processing power and storage capacity; Amazon EC2 instances for the task node type, which don't store data, need only processing power. For guidelines about available Amazon EC2 instances and their configuration, see cite7†Configure Amazon EC2 instance types for use with Amazon EMR .
L25: The following guidelines apply to most Amazon EMR clusters.
L26: 
L27:   * There is a vCPU limit for the total number of on-demand Amazon EC2 instances that you run on an AWS account per AWS Region. For more information about the vCPU limit and how to request a limit increase for your account, see cite8†On-Demand Instances in the Amazon EC2 User Guide for Linux Instances.
L28:   * The primary node does not typically have large computational requirements. For clusters with a large number of nodes, or for clusters with applications that are specifically deployed on the primary node (JupyterHub, Hue, etc.), a larger primary node may be required and can help improve cluster performance. For example, consider using an m5.xlarge instance for small clusters (50 or fewer nodes), and increasing to a larger instance type for larger clusters.
L29:   * The computational needs of the core and task nodes depend on the type of processing your application performs. Many jobs can be run on general purpose instance types, which offer balanced performance in terms of CPU, disk space, and input/output. Computation-intensive clusters may benefit from running on High CPU instances, which have proportionally more CPU than RAM. Database and memory-caching applications may benefit from running on High Memory instances.
L30: Network-intensive and CPU-intensive applications like parsing, NLP, and machine learning may benefit from running on cluster compute instances, which provide proportionally high CPU resources and increased network performance.
L31:   * If different phases of your cluster have different capacity needs, you can start with a small number of core nodes and increase or decrease the number of task nodes to meet your job flow's varying capacity requirements.
L32: 
L33:   * The amount of data you can process depends on the capacity of your core nodes and the size of your data as input, during processing, and as output. The input, intermediate, and output datasets all reside on the cluster during processing.
L34: ## When should you use Spot Instances?
L35: When you launch a cluster in Amazon EMR, you can choose to launch primary, core, or task instances on Spot Instances. Because each type of instance group plays a different role in the cluster, there are implications of launching each node type on Spot Instances. You can't change an instance purchasing option while a cluster is running. To change from On-Demand to Spot Instances or vice versa, for the primary and core nodes, you must terminate the cluster and launch a new one.
L36: For task nodes, you can launch a new task instance group or instance fleet, and remove the old one.
L37: ###### Topics
L38: 
L39:   * cite9†Amazon EMR settings to prevent job failure because of task node Spot Instance termination L40: 
L41:   * cite10†Primary node on a Spot Instance L42: 
L43:   * cite11†Core nodes on Spot Instances L44: 
L45:   * cite12†Task nodes on Spot Instances L46: 
L47:   * cite13†Instance configurations for application scenarios L48: ### Amazon EMR settings to prevent job failure because of task node Spot Instance termination
L49: 
L50: Because Spot Instances are often used to run task nodes, Amazon EMR has default functionality for scheduling YARN jobs so that running jobs do not fail when task nodes running on Spot Instances are terminated. Amazon EMR does this by allowing application master processes to run only on core nodes. The application master process controls running jobs and needs to stay alive for the life of the job.
L51: Amazon EMR release 5.19.0 and later uses the built-in cite14†YARN node labels†hadoop.apache.org feature to achieve this. (Earlier versions used a code patch). Properties in the `yarn-site` and `capacity-scheduler` configuration classifications are configured by default so that the YARN capacity-scheduler and fair-scheduler take advantage of node labels.
L52: Amazon EMR automatically labels core nodes with the `CORE` label, and sets properties so that application masters are scheduled only on nodes with the CORE label. Manually modifying related properties in the yarn-site and capacity-scheduler configuration classifications, or directly in associated XML files, could break this feature or modify this functionality.
L53: Amazon EMR configures the following properties and values by default. Use caution when configuring these properties.
L54: ###### Note
L55: 
L56: Beginning with Amazon EMR 6.x release series, the YARN node labels feature is disabled by default. The application primary processes can run on both core and task nodes by default. You can enable the YARN node labels feature by configuring following properties:
L57: 
L58:   * `yarn.node-labels.enabled: true`
L59: 
L60:   * `yarn.node-labels.am.default-node-label-expression: 'CORE'`
L61: 
L62:   * yarn-site (yarn-site.xml) On All Nodes
L63: 
L64:     * `yarn.node-labels.enabled: true`
L65:     * `yarn.node-labels.am.default-node-label-expression: 'CORE'`
L66: 
L67:     * `yarn.node-labels.fs-store.root-dir: '/apps/yarn/nodelabels'`
L68: 
L69:     * `yarn.node-labels.configuration-type: 'distributed'`
L70: 
L71:   * yarn-site (yarn-site.xml) On Primary And Core Nodes
L72: 
L73:     * `yarn.nodemanager.node-labels.provider: 'config'`
L74: 
L75:     * `yarn.nodemanager.node-labels.provider.configured-node-partition: 'CORE'`
L76: 
L77:   * capacity-scheduler (capacity-scheduler.xml) On All Nodes
L78:     * `yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.accessible-node-labels: '*'`
L79: 
L80:     * `yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.accessible-node-labels.CORE.capacity: 100`
L81: 
L82:     * `yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.default.accessible-node-labels: '*'`
L83: 
L84:     * `yarn.scheduler.capacity.root.default.accessible-node-labels.CORE.capacity: 100`
L85: ### Primary node on a Spot Instance
L86: 
L87: The primary node controls and directs the cluster. When it terminates, the cluster ends, so you should only launch the primary node as a Spot Instance if you are running a cluster where sudden termination is acceptable. This might be the case if you are testing a new application, have a cluster that periodically persists data to an external store such as Amazon S3, or are running a cluster where cost is more important than ensuring the cluster's completion.
L88: When you launch the primary instance group as a Spot Instance, the cluster does not start until that Spot Instance request is fulfilled. This is something to consider when selecting your maximum Spot price.
L89: 
L90: You can only add a Spot Instance primary node when you launch the cluster. You can't add or remove primary nodes from a running cluster.
L91: 
L92: Typically, you would only run the primary node as a Spot Instance if you are running the entire cluster (all instance groups) as Spot Instances.
L93: ### Core nodes on Spot Instances
L94: 
L95: Core nodes process data and store information using HDFS. Terminating a core instance risks data loss. For this reason, you should only run core nodes on Spot Instances when partial HDFS data loss is tolerable.
L96: When you launch the core instance group as Spot Instances, Amazon EMR waits until it can provision all of the requested core instances before launching the instance group. In other words, if you request six Amazon EC2 instances, and only five are available at or below your maximum Spot price, the instance group won't launch. Amazon EMR continues to wait until all six Amazon EC2 instances are available or until you terminate the cluster.
L97: You can change the number of Spot Instances in a core instance group to add capacity to a running cluster. For more information about working with instance groups, and how Spot Instances work with instance fleets, see cite15†Create an Amazon EMR cluster with instance fleets or uniform instance groups .
L98: ### Task nodes on Spot Instances
L99: 
L100: The task nodes process data but do not hold persistent data in HDFS. If they terminate because the Spot price has risen above your maximum Spot price, no data is lost and the effect on your cluster is minimal.
L101: When you launch one or more task instance groups as Spot Instances, Amazon EMR provisions as many task nodes as it can, using your maximum Spot price. This means that if you request a task instance group with six nodes, and only five Spot Instances are available at or below your maximum Spot price, Amazon EMR launches the instance group with five nodes, adding the sixth later if possible.
L102: Launching task instance groups as Spot Instances is a strategic way to expand the capacity of your cluster while minimizing costs. If you launch your primary and core instance groups as On-Demand Instances, their capacity is guaranteed for the run of the cluster. You can add task instances to your task instance groups as needed, to handle peak traffic or speed up data processing.
L103: You can add or remove task nodes using the console, AWS CLI, or API. You can also add additional task groups, but you cannot remove a task group after it is created.
L104: ### Instance configurations for application scenarios
L105: 
L106: The following table is a quick reference to node type purchasing options and configurations that are usually appropriate for various application scenarios. Choose the link to view more information about each scenario type.
L107: Application scenario  | Primary node purchasing option  | Core nodes purchasing option  | Task nodes purchasing option
L108: --- | --- | --- | ---
L109: cite16†Long-running clusters and data warehouses | On-Demand  | On-Demand or instance-fleet mix  | Spot or instance-fleet mix
L110: cite17†Cost-driven workloads | Spot  | Spot  | Spot
L111: cite18†Data-critical workloads | On-Demand  | On-Demand  | Spot or instance-fleet mix
L112: cite19†Application testing | Spot  | Spot  | Spot
L113: There are several scenarios in which Spot Instances are useful for running an Amazon EMR cluster.
L114: #### Long-running clusters and data warehouses
L115: 
L116: If you are running a persistent Amazon EMR cluster that has a predictable variation in computational capacity, such as a data warehouse, you can handle peak demand at lower cost with Spot Instances. You can launch your primary and core instance groups as On-Demand Instances to handle the normal capacity and launch the task instance group as Spot Instances to handle your peak load requirements.
L117: #### Cost-driven workloads
L118: 
L119: If you are running transient clusters for which lower cost is more important than the time to completion, and losing partial work is acceptable, you can run the entire cluster (primary, core, and task instance groups) as Spot Instances to benefit from the largest cost savings.
L120: #### Data-critical workloads
L121: If you are running a cluster for which lower cost is more important than time to completion, but losing partial work is not acceptable, launch the primary and core instance groups as On-Demand Instances and supplement with one or more task instance groups of Spot Instances.
L122: Running the primary and core instance groups as On-Demand Instances ensures that your data is persisted in HDFS and that the cluster is protected from termination due to Spot market fluctuations, while providing cost savings that accrue from running the task instance groups as Spot Instances.
L123: #### Application testing
L124: 
L125: When you are testing a new application in order to prepare it for launch in a production environment, you can run the entire cluster (primary, core, and task instance groups) as Spot Instances to reduce your testing costs.
L126: ## Calculating the required HDFS capacity of a cluster
L127: 
L128: The amount of HDFS storage available to your cluster depends on the following factors:
L129: 
L130:   * The number of Amazon EC2 instances used for core nodes.
L131: 
L132:   * The capacity of the Amazon EC2 instance store for the instance type used. For more information on instance store volumes, see cite20†Amazon Amazon EC2 instance store in the Amazon EC2 User Guide.
L133: 
L134:   * The number and size of Amazon EBS volumes attached to core nodes.
L135:   * A replication factor, which accounts for how each data block is stored in HDFS for RAID-like redundancy. By default, the replication factor is three for a cluster of 10 or more core nodes, two for a cluster of 4-9 core nodes, and one for a cluster of three or fewer nodes.
L136: To calculate the HDFS capacity of a cluster, for each core node, add the instance store volume capacity to the Amazon EBS storage capacity (if used). Multiply the result by the number of core nodes, and then divide the total by the replication factor based on the number of core nodes.
L137: For example, a cluster with 10 core nodes of type i2.xlarge, which have 800 GB of instance storage without any attached Amazon EBS volumes, has a total of approximately 2,666 GB available for HDFS (10 nodes x 800 GB ÷ 3 replication factor).
L138: If the calculated HDFS capacity value is smaller than your data, you can increase the amount of HDFS storage in the following ways:
L139: 
L140:   * Creating a cluster with additional Amazon EBS volumes or adding instance groups with attached Amazon EBS volumes to an existing cluster
L141: 
L142:   * Adding more core nodes
L143: 
L144:   * Choosing an Amazon EC2 instance type with greater storage capacity
L145: 
L146:   * Using data compression
L147: 
L148:   * Changing the Hadoop configuration settings to reduce the replication factor
L149: Reducing the replication factor should be used with caution as it reduces the redundancy of HDFS data and the ability of the cluster to recover from lost or corrupted HDFS blocks.

L4: cite1†Network Isolation L5: # Run Training and Inference Containers in Internet-Free Mode
L6: SageMaker AI training and deployed inference containers are internet-enabled by default. This allows containers to access external services and resources on the public internet as part of your training and inference workloads. However, this could provide an avenue for unauthorized access to your data. For example, a malicious user or code that you accidentally install on the container (in the form of a publicly available source code library) could access your data and transfer it to a remote host.
L7: If you use an Amazon VPC by specifying a value for the `VpcConfig` parameter when you call cite2†`CreateTrainingJob` , cite3†`CreateHyperParameterTuningJob` , or cite4†`CreateModel` , you can protect your data and resources by managing security groups and restricting internet access from your VPC. However, this comes at the cost of additional network configuration, and has the risk of configuring your network incorrectly.
L8: If you do not want SageMaker AI to provide external network access to your training or inference containers, you can enable network isolation.
L9: ## Network Isolation
L10: 
L11: You can enable network isolation when you create your training job or model by setting the value of the `EnableNetworkIsolation` parameter to `True` when you call cite2†`CreateTrainingJob` , cite3†`CreateHyperParameterTuningJob` , or cite4†`CreateModel` .
L12: ###### Note
L13: 
L14: Network isolation is required to run training jobs and models using resources from AWS Marketplace. For additional security, AWS Marketplace images run within an Amazon VPC. They only have access to data within their local file systems.
L15: When you enable network isolation, your training and inference containers can't make any outbound network calls to any service, including Amazon S3. No AWS credentials are made available to the container runtime environment. For training jobs with multiple instances, network inbound and outbound traffic is limited to communication between training container peers.
L16: SageMaker AI still handles all necessary Amazon S3 download and upload operations using your SageMaker AI execution role. This happens apart from your training and inference containers, ensuring that your training data and model artifacts are still accessible while maintaining container isolation.
L17: 
L18: The following managed SageMaker AI containers do not support network isolation because they require access to Amazon S3:
L19: 
L20:   * Chainer
L21: 
L22:   * SageMaker AI Reinforcement Learning
L23: ### Network isolation with a VPC
L24: 
L25: Network isolation can be used in conjunction with a VPC. In this scenario, the download and upload of customer data and model artifacts are routed through your VPC subnet. However, the training and inference containers themselves continue to be isolated from the network, and do not have access to any resource within your VPC or on the internet.

L2: What is Amazon Athena? - Amazon Athena
L3: # What is Amazon Athena?
L4: 
L5: Amazon Athena is an interactive query service that makes it easy to analyze data directly in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) using standard cite1†SQL . With a few actions in the AWS Management Console, you can point Athena at your data stored in Amazon S3 and begin using standard SQL to run ad-hoc queries and get results in seconds.
L6: 
L7: For more information, see cite2†Get started .
L8: Amazon Athena also makes it easy to interactively run data analytics using Apache Spark without having to plan for, configure, or manage resources. When you run Apache Spark applications on Athena, you submit Spark code for processing and receive the results directly. Use the simplified notebook experience in Amazon Athena console to develop Apache Spark applications using Python or cite3†Use Athena Spark APIs .
L9: 
L10: For more information, see cite4†Get started with Apache Spark on Amazon Athena .
L11: Athena SQL and Apache Spark on Amazon Athena are serverless, so there is no infrastructure to set up or manage, and you pay only for the queries you run. Athena scales automatically—running queries in parallel—so results are fast, even with large datasets and complex queries.

L6: # Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Terminology and concepts
L7: 
L8: Before you get started with Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, learn about its architecture and terminology.
L9: ###### Topics
L10: 
L11:   * cite1†Review the high-level architecture of Kinesis Data Streams L12: 
L13:   * cite2†Become familiar with the terminology of Kinesis Data Streams L14: ## Review the high-level architecture of Kinesis Data Streams
L15: 
L16: The following diagram illustrates the high-level architecture of Kinesis Data Streams. The producers continually push data to Kinesis Data Streams, and the consumers process the data in real time. Consumers (such as a custom application running on Amazon EC2 or an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream) can store their results using an AWS service such as Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Redshift, or Amazon S3.
L17: cite3†Image: Kinesis Data Streams high-level architecture diagram L18: ## Become familiar with the terminology of Kinesis Data Streams
L19: 
L20: ### Kinesis Data Stream
L21: 
L22: A Kinesis data stream is a set of cite4†shards . Each shard has a sequence of data records. Each data record has a cite5†sequence number that is assigned by Kinesis Data Streams.
L23: ### Data Record
L24: 
L25: A data record is the unit of data stored in a cite6†Kinesis data stream . Data records are composed of a cite5†sequence number , a cite7†partition key , and a data blob, which is an immutable sequence of bytes. Kinesis Data Streams does not inspect, interpret, or change the data in the blob in any way. A data blob can be up to 1 MB.
L26: ### Capacity Mode
L27: 
L28: A data stream capacity mode determines how capacity is managed and how you are charged for the usage of your data stream. Currently, in Kinesis Data Streams, you can choose between an on-demand mode and a provisioned mode for your data streams. For more information, see cite8†Choose the right mode to stream in .
L29: With the on-demand mode, Kinesis Data Streams automatically manages the shards in order to provide the necessary throughput. You are charged only for the actual throughput that you use and Kinesis Data Streams automatically accommodates your workloads’ throughput needs as they ramp up or down. For more information, see cite9†On-demand Standard mode features and use cases .
L30: With the provisioned mode, you must specify the number of shards for the data stream. The total capacity of a data stream is the sum of the capacities of its shards. You can increase or decrease the number of shards in a data stream as needed and you are charged for the number of shards at an hourly rate. For more information, see cite10†Provisioned mode features and use cases .
L31: ### Retention Period
L32: The retention period is the length of time that data records are accessible after they are added to the stream. A stream’s retention period is set to a default of 24 hours after creation. You can increase the retention period up to 8760 hours (365 days) using the cite11†IncreaseStreamRetentionPeriod operation, and decrease the retention period down to a minimum of 24 hours using the cite12†DecreaseStreamRetentionPeriod operation.
L33: Additional charges apply for streams with a retention period set to more than 24 hours. For more information, see cite13†Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L34: ### Producer
L35: 
L36: Producers put records into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. For example, a web server sending log data to a stream is a producer.
L37: 
L38: ### Consumer
L39: 
L40: Consumers get records from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and process them. These consumers are known as cite14†Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Application .
L41: ### Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Application
L42: 
L43: An Amazon Kinesis Data Streams application is a consumer of a stream that commonly runs on a fleet of EC2 instances.
L44: 
L45: There are two types of consumers that you can develop: shared fan-out consumers and enhanced fan-out consumers. To learn about the differences between them, and to see how you can create each type of consumer, see cite15†Read data from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams .
L46: The output of a Kinesis Data Streams application can be input for another stream, enabling you to create complex topologies that process data in real time. An application can also send data to a variety of other AWS services. There can be multiple applications for one stream, and each application can consume data from the stream independently and concurrently.
L47: ### Shard
L48: A shard is a uniquely identified sequence of data records in a stream. A stream is composed of one or more shards, each of which provides a fixed unit of capacity. Each shard can support up to 5 transactions per second for reads, up to a maximum total data read rate of 2 MB per second and up to 1,000 records per second for writes, up to a maximum total data write rate of 1 MB per second (including partition keys).
L49: The data capacity of your stream is a function of the number of shards that you specify for the stream. The total capacity of the stream is the sum of the capacities of its shards.
L50: If your data rate increases, you can increase or decrease the number of shards allocated to your stream. For more information, see cite16†Reshard a stream .
L51: ### Partition Key
L52: A partition key is used to group data by shard within a stream. Kinesis Data Streams segregates the data records belonging to a stream into multiple shards. It uses the partition key that is associated with each data record to determine which shard a given data record belongs to. Partition keys are Unicode strings, with a maximum length limit of 256 characters for each key.
L53: An MD5 hash function is used to map partition keys to 128-bit integer values and to map associated data records to shards using the hash key ranges of the shards. When an application puts data into a stream, it must specify a partition key.
L54: ### Sequence Number
L55: 
L56: Each data record has a sequence number that is unique per partition-key within its shard. Kinesis Data Streams assigns the sequence number after you write to the stream with `client.putRecords` or `client.putRecord`. Sequence numbers for the same partition key generally increase over time. The longer the time period between write requests, the larger the sequence numbers become.
L57: ###### Note
L58: 
L59: Sequence numbers cannot be used as indexes to sets of data within the same stream. To logically separate sets of data, use partition keys or create a separate stream for each dataset.
L60: ### Kinesis Client Library
L61: Kinesis Client Library is compiled into your application to enable fault-tolerant consumption of data from the stream. Kinesis Client Library makes sure that for every shard there is a record processor running and processing that shard. The library also simplifies reading data from the stream. Kinesis Client Library uses Amazon DynamoDB tables to store metadata related to data consumption. It creates three tables per application that is processing data.
L62: For more information, see cite17†Use Kinesis Client Library .
L63: ### Application Name
L64: 
L65: The name of an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams application identifies the application. Each of your applications must have a unique name that is scoped to the AWS account and Region used by the application. This name is used as a name for the control table in Amazon DynamoDB and the namespace for Amazon CloudWatch metrics.
L66: ### Server-Side Encryption
L67: 
L68: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams can automatically encrypt sensitive data as a producer enters it into a stream. Kinesis Data Streams uses cite18†AWS KMS master keys for encryption. For more information, see cite19†Data protection in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams .
L69: ###### Note
L70: 
L71: To read from or write to an encrypted stream, producer and consumer applications must have permission to access the master key. For information about granting permissions to producer and consumer applications, see cite20†Permissions to use user-generated KMS keys .
L72: 
L73: ###### Note
L74: 
L75: Using server-side encryption incurs AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) costs. For more information, see cite21†AWS Key Management Service Pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L76: ### Data delivery
L77: Data delivery is a fully managed capability that delivers streaming data from a Kinesis data stream to an analytics or storage destination without any infrastructure to manage. There are no connectors, consumer applications, or compute resources to provision. Kinesis Data Streams reads from your stream, buffers and aggregates records, and delivers them to your configured destination within minutes.
L78: Data delivery supports two destination types: streaming tables on Apache Iceberg, and general purpose Amazon S3 buckets. For more information, see cite22†Streaming tables and S3 delivery for Amazon Kinesis Data Streams .
L79: #### Delivery to streaming tables in Iceberg format
L80: Continuously materialize streaming data as queryable Apache Iceberg tables on Amazon S3 Tables with no ETL pipeline required. Delivery to streaming tables continuously materializes stream records as Apache Iceberg tables on Amazon S3 Tables. Built-in intelligent inline compaction eliminates small file proliferation and keeps query performance predictable without sacrificing data freshness.
L81: Query or transform data with any engine, including Apache Spark, Trino, Apache Flink, or Amazon Athena, for real-time analytics directly on your streaming data.
L82: #### Delivery to Amazon S3
L83: Deliver streaming data in source format to Amazon S3 buckets for backup, archival, and downstream data processing. Delivery to Amazon S3 delivers streaming records directly to general purpose Amazon S3 buckets in the original source format. Use this capability for long-term data retention, compliance archival, replay and reprocessing workflows, or as a staging layer for downstream batch processing pipelines.
L84: Combined with delivery to streaming tables, you can build a complete lakehouse architecture with real-time queryable tables for analytics alongside full-fidelity raw backup in Amazon S3.

citeturn25view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 3 weeks ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/columnar-storage.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 61

L2: Use columnar storage formats - Amazon Athena
L3: 
L4: cite1†Choose between Parquet and ORC cite2†Convert to columnar formats L5: # Use columnar storage formats
L6: 
L7: cite3†Apache Parquet†parquet.apache.org and cite4†ORC†orc.apache.org are columnar storage formats that are optimized for fast retrieval of data and used in AWS analytical applications.
L8: 
L9: Columnar storage formats have the following characteristics that make them suitable for using with Athena:
L10: 
L11:   * Compression by column, with compression algorithm selected for the column data type to save storage space in Amazon S3 and reduce disk space and I/O during query processing.
L12:   * Predicate pushdown in Parquet and ORC enables Athena queries to fetch only the blocks it needs, improving query performance. When an Athena query obtains specific column values from your data, it uses statistics from data block predicates, such as max/min values, to determine whether to read or skip the block.
L13: 
L14:   * Splitting of data in Parquet and ORC allows Athena to split the reading of data to multiple readers and increase parallelism during its query processing.
L15: To convert your existing raw data from other storage formats to Parquet or ORC, you can run cite5†CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) queries in Athena and specify a data storage format as Parquet or ORC, or use the AWS Glue Crawler.
L16: ## Choose between Parquet and ORC
L17: 
L18: The choice between ORC (Optimized Row Columnar) and Parquet depends on your specific usage requirements.
L19: 
L20: Apache Parquet provides efficient data compression and encoding schemes and is ideal for running complex queries and processing large amounts of data. Parquet is optimized for use with cite6†Apache Arrow†arrow.apache.org , which can be advantageous if you use tools that are Arrow related.
L21: ORC provides an efficient way to store Hive data. ORC files are often smaller than Parquet files, and ORC indexes can make querying faster. In addition, ORC supports complex types such as structs, maps, and lists.
L22: 
L23: When choosing between Parquet and ORC, consider the following:
L24: 
L25: Query performance – Because Parquet supports a wider range of query types, Parquet might be a better choice if you plan to perform complex queries.
L26: Complex data types – If you are using complex data types, ORC might be a better choice as it supports a wider range of complex data types.
L27: 
L28: File size – If disk space is a concern, ORC usually results in smaller files, which can reduce storage costs.
L29: 
L30: Compression – Both Parquet and ORC provide good compression, but the best format for you can depend on your specific use case.
L31: 
L32: Evolution – Both Parquet and ORC support schema evolution, which means you can add, remove, or modify columns over time.
L33: Both Parquet and ORC are good choices for big data applications, but consider the requirements of your scenario before choosing. You might want to perform benchmarks on your data and queries to see which format performs better for your use case.
L34: ## Convert to columnar formats
L35: 
L36: Options for easily converting source data such as JSON or CSV into a columnar format include using cite5†CREATE TABLE AS queries or running jobs in AWS Glue.
L37: 
L38:   * You can use `CREATE TABLE AS` (CTAS) queries to convert data into Parquet or ORC in one step. For an example, see cite7†Example: Writing query results to a different format on the cite8†Examples of CTAS queries page.
L39:   * For information about using Athena for ETL to transform data from CSV to Parquet, see cite9†Use CTAS and INSERT INTO for ETL and data analysis .
L40:   * For information about running an AWS Glue job to transform CSV data to Parquet, see the section "Transform the data from CSV to Parquet format" in the AWS Big Data blog post cite10†Build a data lake foundation with AWS Glue and Amazon S3†aws.amazon.com . AWS Glue supports using the same technique to convert CSV data to ORC, or JSON data to either Parquet or ORC.

L6: # Customization of a SageMaker notebook instance using an LCC script
L7: ###### Important
L8: Custom IAM policies that allow Amazon SageMaker Studio or Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic to create Amazon SageMaker resources must also grant permissions to add tags to those resources. The permission to add tags to resources is required because Studio and Studio Classic automatically tag any resources they create. If an IAM policy allows Studio and Studio Classic to create resources but does not allow tagging, "AccessDenied" errors can occur when trying to create resources.
L9: For more information, see cite2†Provide permissions for tagging SageMaker AI resources .
L10: cite3†AWS managed policies for Amazon SageMaker AI that give permissions to create SageMaker resources already include permissions to add tags while creating those resources.
L11: 
L12: A lifecycle configuration (LCC) provides shell scripts that run only when you create the notebook instance or whenever you start one. When you create a notebook instance, you can create a new LCC or attach an LCC that you already have. Lifecycle configuration scripts are useful for the following use cases:
L13:   * Installing packages or sample notebooks on a notebook instance
L14: 
L15:   * Configuring networking and security for a notebook instance
L16: 
L17:   * Using a shell script to customize a notebook instance
L18: 
L19: You can also use a lifecycle configuration script to access AWS services from your notebook. For example, you can create a script that lets you use your notebook to control other AWS resources, such as an Amazon EMR instance.
L20: We maintain a public repository of notebook lifecycle configuration scripts that address common use cases for customizing notebook instances at cite4†https://github.com/aws-samples/amazon-sagemaker-notebook-instance-lifecycle-config-samples†github.com .
L21: ###### Note
L22: 
L23: Each script has a limit of 16384 characters.
L24: 
L25: The value of the `$PATH` environment variable that is available to both scripts is `/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin:/bin`. The working directory, which is the value of the `$PWD` environment variable, is `/`.
L26: 
L27: View CloudWatch Logs for notebook instance lifecycle configurations in log group `/aws/sagemaker/NotebookInstances` in log stream `[notebook-instance-name]/[LifecycleConfigHook]`.
L28: Scripts cannot run for longer than 5 minutes. If a script runs for longer than 5 minutes, it fails and the notebook instance is not created or started. To help decrease the run time of scripts, try the following:
L29: 
L30:   * Cut down on necessary steps. For example, limit which conda environments in which to install large packages.
L31: 
L32:   * Run tasks in parallel processes.
L33: 
L34:   * Use the `nohup` command in your script.
L35: You can see a list of notebook instance lifecycle configurations you previously created by choosing Lifecycle configuration in the SageMaker AI console. You can attach a notebook instance LCC when you create a new notebook instance. For more information about creating a notebook instance, see cite5†Create an Amazon SageMaker notebook instance .
L36: ## Lifecycle Configuration Best Practices
L37: 
L38: The following are best practices for using lifecycle configurations:
L39: 
L40: ###### Important
L41: 
L42: We do not recommend storing sensitive information in your lifecycle configuration script.
L43: ###### Important
L44: 
L45: Lifecycle configuration scripts run with root access and the notebook instance's IAM execution role privileges, regardless of the root access setting for notebook users. Principals with permissions to create or modify lifecycle configurations and update notebook instances can execute code with the execution role's credentials. See cite6†Control root access to a SageMaker notebook instance for more information.
L46:   * Lifecycle configurations run as the `root` user. If your script makes any changes within the `/home/ec2-user/SageMaker` directory, (for example, installing a package with `pip`), use the command `sudo -u ec2-user` to run as the `ec2-user` user. This is the same user that Amazon SageMaker AI runs as.
L47:   * SageMaker AI notebook instances use `conda` environments to implement different kernels for Jupyter notebooks. If you want to install packages that are available to one or more notebook kernels, enclose the commands to install the packages with `conda` environment commands that activate the conda environment that contains the kernel where you want to install the packages.
L48: For example, if you want to install a package only for the `python3` environment, use the following code:
L49: 
L50:     `#!/bin/bash
L51:     sudo -u ec2-user -i <<EOF
L52: 
L53:     # This will affect only the Jupyter kernel called "conda_python3".
L54:     source activate python3
L55: 
L56:     # Replace `myPackage` with the name of the package you want to install.
L57:     pip install `myPackage`
L58:     # You can also perform "conda install" here as well.
L59: 
L60:     source deactivate
L61: 
L62:     EOF`
L63: If you want to install a package in all conda environments in the notebook instance, use the following code:
L64: 
L65:     `#!/bin/bash
L66:     sudo -u ec2-user -i <<EOF
L67: 
L68:     # Note that "base" is special environment name, include it there as well.
L69:     for env in base /home/ec2-user/anaconda3/envs/*; do
L70:         source /home/ec2-user/anaconda3/bin/activate $(basename "$env")
L71: 
L72:         # Installing packages in the Jupyter system environment can affect stability of your SageMaker
L73:         # Notebook Instance.  You can remove this check if you'd like to install Jupyter extensions, etc.
L74:         if [ $env = 'JupyterSystemEnv' ]; then
L75:           continue
L76:         fi
L77: 
L78:         # Replace `myPackage` with the name of the package you want to install.
L79:         pip install --upgrade --quiet `myPackage`
L80:         # You can also perform "conda install" here as well.
L81: 
L82:         source /home/ec2-user/anaconda3/bin/deactivate
L83:     done
L84: 
L85:     EOF`
L86:   * You must store all conda environments in the default environments folder (/home/user/anaconda3/envs).
L87: ###### Important
L88: 
L89: When you create or change a script, we recommend that you use a text editor that provides Unix-style line breaks, such as the text editor available in the console when you create a notebook. Copying text from a non-Linux operating system might introduce incompatible line breaks and result in an unexpected error.

L2: Data discovery and cataloging in AWS Glue - AWS Glue
L3: # Data discovery and cataloging in AWS Glue
L4: 
L5: The AWS Glue Data Catalog is a centralized repository that stores metadata about your organization's data sets. It acts as an index to the location, schema, and runtime metrics of your data sources. The metadata is stored in metadata tables, where each table represents a single data store.
L6: You can populate the Data Catalog using a crawler, which automatically scans your data sources and extracts metadata. A crawler can connect to data sources that are internal (AWS-based) and external to AWS.
L7: 
L8: For more information about the supported data sources, see cite1†Supported data sources for crawling L9: 
L10: You can also create tables in the Data Catalog manually by defining the table structure, schema, and partitioning structure according to your specific requirements.
L11: For more information about creating metadata tables manually, see cite2†Defining metadata manually .
L12: 
L13: You can use the information in the Data Catalog to create and monitor your ETL jobs. The Data Catalog integrates with other AWS analytics services, providing a unified view of data sources making it easier to manage and analyze data.
L14: 
L15:   * Amazon Athena – Store and query table metadata in the Data Catalog for the Amazon S3 data using SQL.
L16:   * AWS Lake Formation – Centrally define and manage fine-grained data access policies and audit data access.
L17: 
L18:   * Amazon EMR – Access data sources defined in the Data Catalog for big data processing.
L19: 
L20:   * Amazon SageMaker AI – Quickly and confidently build, train, and deploy machine learning models.
L21: ###### Key features of the Data Catalog
L22: 
L23: The following are the key aspects of the Data Catalog.
L24: 
L25: Metadata repository
L26: 
L27: 
L28: The Data Catalog acts as a central metadata repository, storing information about the location, schema, and properties of your data sources. This metadata is organized into databases and tables, similar to a traditional relational database catalog.
L29: 
L30: Automatic data discoverability
L31: AWS Glue crawlers can automatically discover and catalog new or updated data sources, reducing the overhead of manual metadata management and ensuring that your Data Catalog remains up-to-date. By cataloging your data sources, the Data Catalog makes it easier for users and applications to discover and understand the available data assets within your organization, promoting data reuse and collaboration.
L32: The Data Catalog supports a wide range of data sources, including Amazon S3, Amazon RDS, Amazon Redshift, Apache Hive, and more. It can automatically infer and store metadata from these sources using AWS Glue crawlers.
L33: 
L34: For more information see, cite3†Using crawlers to populate the Data Catalog .
L35: 
L36: Schema management
L37: The Data Catalog automatically captures and manages the schema of your data sources, including schema inference, evolution, and versioning. You can update your schema and partitions in the Data Catalog using AWS Glue ETL jobs.
L38: 
L39: Table optimization
L40: For better read performance by AWS analytics services such as Amazon Athena and Amazon EMR, and AWS Glue ETL jobs, the Data Catalog provides managed compaction (a process that compacts small Amazon S3 objects into larger objects) for Iceberg tables in the Data Catalog. You can use AWS Glue console, AWS Lake Formation console, AWS CLI, or AWS API to enable or disable compaction for individual Iceberg tables that are in the Data Catalog.
L41: 
L42: For more information, see cite4†Optimizing Iceberg tables .
L43: Column statistics
L44: 
L45: 
L46: You can compute column-level statistics for Data Catalog tables in data formats such as Parquet, ORC, JSON, ION, CSV, and XML without setting up additional data pipelines. Column statistics help you to understand data profiles by getting insights about values within a column. The Data Catalog supports generating statistics for column values such as minimum value, maximum value, total null values, total distinct values, average length of values, and total occurrences of true values.
L47: For more information, see cite5†Optimizing query performance using column statistics .
L48: 
L49: Data lineage
L50: 
L51: 
L52: The Data Catalog maintains a record of the transformations and operations performed on your data, providing data lineage information. This lineage information is valuable for auditing, compliance, and understanding the data's provenance.
L53: 
L54: Integration with other AWS services
L55: The Data Catalog seamlessly integrates with other AWS services, such as AWS Lake Formation, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift Spectrum, and Amazon EMR. This integration allows you to query and analyze data across various data stores using a single, consistent metadata layer.
L56: 
L57: Security and access control
L58: AWS Glue integrates with AWS Lake Formation to support fine-grained access control for Data Catalog resources, allowing you to manage permissions and secure access to your data assets based on your organization's policies and requirements. AWS Glue integrates with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to encrypt metadata that's stored in the Data Catalog.
L59: 
L60: Business context and semantic search (Preview)
L61: Enrich Data Catalog assets with glossary terms, custom metadata fields, and skill assets to make data more discoverable. Use the AWS Glue Search API to find assets by semantic meaning in addition to exact keyword matching. AI agents can use skill assets to retrieve domain context such as query patterns, usage rules, and data definitions.
L62: 
L63: For more information, see cite6†Adding business context .
L64: 
L65: Materialized views
L66: The Data Catalog supports Apache Iceberg materialized views, which are managed tables that store precomputed results of SQL queries and automatically refresh as underlying source data changes. Materialized views simplify data transformation pipelines and accelerate query performance by eliminating redundant computation.
L67: You can create materialized views using Apache Spark SQL in AWS Glue version 5.1 and later, Amazon EMR release 7.12.0 and later, and Amazon Athena. The Data Catalog automatically monitors source Apache Iceberg tables and refreshes materialized views using managed compute infrastructure. Spark engines across AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, and Amazon Athena can automatically rewrite queries to use materialized views when they provide better performance.
L68: Materialized views are stored as Apache Iceberg tables in Amazon S3 Tables buckets or Amazon S3 general purpose buckets within your account, making them accessible from multiple query engines. The Data Catalog manages all aspects of materialized view lifecycle, including automatic refresh scheduling, incremental updates, and metadata management.
L69: 
L70: For more information, see Using materialized views with AWS Glue and Using materialized views with Amazon EMR.

L3: 
L4: cite1†Request Syntax cite2†Request Parameters cite3†Response Syntax cite4†Response Elements cite5†Errors cite6†See Also L5: 
L6: # CreatePredictor
L7: 
L8: ###### Note
L9: 
L10: This operation creates a legacy predictor that does not include all the predictor functionalities provided by Amazon Forecast. To create a predictor that is compatible with all aspects of Forecast, use cite7†CreateAutoPredictor .
L11: 
L12: Creates an Amazon Forecast predictor.
L13: ###### Important
L14: 
L15: Amazon Forecast is no longer available to new customers. Existing customers of Amazon Forecast can continue to use the service as normal. cite8†Learn more"†aws.amazon.com L16: 
L17: In the request, provide a dataset group and either specify an algorithm or let Amazon Forecast choose an algorithm for you using AutoML. If you specify an algorithm, you also can override algorithm-specific hyperparameters.
L18: Amazon Forecast uses the algorithm to train a predictor using the latest version of the datasets in the specified dataset group. You can then generate a forecast using the cite9†CreateForecast operation.
L19: 
L20: To see the evaluation metrics, use the cite10†GetAccuracyMetrics operation.
L21: 
L22: You can specify a featurization configuration to fill and aggregate the data fields in the `TARGET_TIME_SERIES` dataset to improve model training. For more information, see cite11†FeaturizationConfig .
L23: For RELATED_TIME_SERIES datasets, `CreatePredictor` verifies that the `DataFrequency` specified when the dataset was created matches the `ForecastFrequency`. TARGET_TIME_SERIES datasets don't have this restriction. Amazon Forecast also verifies the delimiter and timestamp format. For more information, see cite12†Importing Datasets .
L24: By default, predictors are trained and evaluated at the 0.1 (P10), 0.5 (P50), and 0.9 (P90) quantiles. You can choose custom forecast types to train and evaluate your predictor by setting the `ForecastTypes`.
L25: 
L26: AutoML
L27: If you want Amazon Forecast to evaluate each algorithm and choose the one that minimizes the `objective function`, set `PerformAutoML` to `true`. The `objective function` is defined as the mean of the weighted losses over the forecast types. By default, these are the p10, p50, and p90 quantile losses. For more information, see cite13†EvaluationResult .
L28: 
L29: When AutoML is enabled, the following properties are disallowed:
L30: 
L31:   * `AlgorithmArn`
L32: 
L33:   * `HPOConfig`
L34: 
L35:   * `PerformHPO`
L36: 
L37:   * `TrainingParameters`
L38: To get a list of all of your predictors, use the cite14†ListPredictors operation.
L39: ###### Note
L40: 
L41: Before you can use the predictor to create a forecast, the `Status` of the predictor must be `ACTIVE`, signifying that training has completed. To get the status, use the cite15†DescribePredictor operation.
L42: ## Request Syntax
L43: 
L44:     `{
L45:        "cite16†AlgorithmArn ": "`string`",
L46:        "cite17†AutoMLOverrideStrategy ": "`string`",
L47:        "cite18†EncryptionConfig ": {
L48:           "cite19†KMSKeyArn ": "`string`",
L49:           "cite20†RoleArn ": "`string`"
L50:        },
L51:        "cite21†EvaluationParameters ": {
L52:           "cite22†BackTestWindowOffset ": `number`,
L53:           "cite23†NumberOfBacktestWindows ": `number`
L54:        },
L55:        "cite24†FeaturizationConfig ": {
L56:           "cite25†Featurizations ": [
L57:              {
L58:                 "cite26†AttributeName ": "`string`",
L59:                 "cite27†FeaturizationPipeline ": [
L60:                    {
L61:                       "cite28†FeaturizationMethodName ": "`string`",
L62:                       "cite29†FeaturizationMethodParameters ": {
L63:                          "`string`" : "`string`"
L64:                       }
L65:                    }
L66:                 ]
L67:              }
L68:           ],
L69:           "cite30†ForecastDimensions ": [ "`string`" ],
L70:           "cite31†ForecastFrequency ": "`string`"
L71:        },
L72:        "cite32†ForecastHorizon ": `number`,
L73:        "cite33†ForecastTypes ": [ "`string`" ],
L74:        "cite34†HPOConfig ": {
L75:           "cite35†ParameterRanges ": {
L76:              "cite36†CategoricalParameterRanges ": [
L77:                 {
L78:                    "cite37†Name ": "`string`",
L79:                    "cite38†Values ": [ "`string`" ]
L80:                 }
L81:              ],
L82:              "cite39†ContinuousParameterRanges ": [
L83:                 {
L84:                    "cite40†MaxValue ": `number`,
L85:                    "cite41†MinValue ": `number`,
L86:                    "cite42†Name ": "`string`",
L87:                    "cite43†ScalingType ": "`string`"
L88:                 }
L89:              ],

L91:                 {
L92:                    "cite45†MaxValue ": `number`,
L93:                    "cite46†MinValue ": `number`,
L94:                    "cite47†Name ": "`string`",

L106:              }
L107:           ]
L108:        },
L109:        "cite54†OptimizationMetric ": "`string`",
L110:        "cite55†PerformAutoML ": `boolean`,
L111:        "cite56†PerformHPO ": `boolean`,
L112:        "cite57†PredictorName ": "`string`",

L114:           {

L117:           }
L118:        ],
L119:        "cite61†TrainingParameters ": {
L120:           "`string`" : "`string`"
L121:        }
L122:     }`
L123: ## Request Parameters
L124: 
L125: The request accepts the following data in JSON format.
L126: 
L127: cite1†AlgorithmArn L128: 
L129: 
L130: The Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the algorithm to use for model training. Required if `PerformAutoML` is not set to `true`.
L131: ###### Supported algorithms:
L132: 
L133:   * `arn:aws:forecast:::algorithm/ARIMA`
L134: 
L135:   * `arn:aws:forecast:::algorithm/CNN-QR`
L136: 
L137:   * `arn:aws:forecast:::algorithm/Deep_AR_Plus`
L138: 
L139:   * `arn:aws:forecast:::algorithm/ETS`
L140: 
L141:   * `arn:aws:forecast:::algorithm/NPTS`
L142: 
L143:   * `arn:aws:forecast:::algorithm/Prophet`
L144: 
L145: Type: String
L146: 
L147: Length Constraints: Maximum length of 256.
L148: 
L149: Pattern: `arn:([a-z\d-]+):forecast:.*:.*:.+`
L150: 
L151: Required: No
L152: 
L153: cite1†AutoMLOverrideStrategy L154: ###### Note
L155: 
L156: The `LatencyOptimized` AutoML override strategy is only available in private beta. Contact AWS Support or your account manager to learn more about access privileges.
L157: 
L158: Used to overide the default AutoML strategy, which is to optimize predictor accuracy. To apply an AutoML strategy that minimizes training time, use `LatencyOptimized`.
L159: 
L160: This parameter is only valid for predictors trained using AutoML.
L161: 
L162: Type: String
L163: 
L164: Valid Values: `LatencyOptimized | AccuracyOptimized`
L165: 
L166: Required: No
L167: cite1†EncryptionConfig L168: 
L169: 
L170: An AWS Key Management Service (KMS) key and the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that Amazon Forecast can assume to access the key.
L171: 
L172: Type: cite62†EncryptionConfig object
L173: 
L174: Required: No
L175: 
L176: cite1†EvaluationParameters L177: Used to override the default evaluation parameters of the specified algorithm. Amazon Forecast evaluates a predictor by splitting a dataset into training data and testing data. The evaluation parameters define how to perform the split and the number of iterations.
L178: 
L179: Type: cite63†EvaluationParameters object
L180: 
L181: Required: No
L182: 
L183: cite1†FeaturizationConfig L184: 
L185: 
L186: The featurization configuration.
L187: 
L188: Type: cite11†FeaturizationConfig object
L189: 
L190: Required: Yes
L191: 
L192: cite1†ForecastHorizon L193: Specifies the number of time-steps that the model is trained to predict. The forecast horizon is also called the prediction length.
L194: 
L195: For example, if you configure a dataset for daily data collection (using the `DataFrequency` parameter of the cite64†CreateDataset operation) and set the forecast horizon to 10, the model returns predictions for 10 days.
L196: 
L197: The maximum forecast horizon is the lesser of 500 time-steps or 1/3 of the TARGET_TIME_SERIES dataset length.
L198: 
L199: Type: Integer
L200: 
L201: Required: Yes
L202: cite1†ForecastTypes L203: 
L204: 
L205: Specifies the forecast types used to train a predictor. You can specify up to five forecast types. Forecast types can be quantiles from 0.01 to 0.99, by increments of 0.01 or higher. You can also specify the mean forecast with `mean`.
L206: 
L207: The default value is `["0.10", "0.50", "0.9"]`.
L208: 
L209: Type: Array of strings
L210: 
L211: Array Members: Minimum number of 1 item. Maximum number of 20 items.
L212: 
L213: Length Constraints: Minimum length of 2. Maximum length of 4.
L214: 
L215: Pattern: `(^0?\.\d\d?$|^mean$)`
L216: Required: No
L217: 
L218: cite1†HPOConfig L219: 
L220: 
L221: Provides hyperparameter override values for the algorithm. If you don't provide this parameter, Amazon Forecast uses default values. The individual algorithms specify which hyperparameters support hyperparameter optimization (HPO). For more information, see cite65†Amazon Forecast Algorithms .
L222: 
L223: If you included the `HPOConfig` object, you must set `PerformHPO` to true.
L224: 
L225: Type: cite66†HyperParameterTuningJobConfig object
L226: 
L227: Required: No
L228: 
L229: cite1†InputDataConfig L230: Describes the dataset group that contains the data to use to train the predictor.
L231: 
L232: Type: cite67†InputDataConfig object
L233: 
L234: Required: Yes
L235: 
L236: cite1†OptimizationMetric L237: 
L238: 
L239: The accuracy metric used to optimize the predictor. The default value is `AverageWeightedQuantileLoss`.
L240: 
L241: Type: String
L242: 
L243: Valid Values: `WAPE | RMSE | AverageWeightedQuantileLoss | MASE | MAPE`
L244: 
L245: Required: No
L246: 
L247: cite1†PerformAutoML L248: Whether to perform AutoML. When Amazon Forecast performs AutoML, it evaluates the algorithms it provides and chooses the best algorithm and configuration for your training dataset.
L249: 
L250: The default value is `false`. In this case, you are required to specify an algorithm.
L251: 
L252: Set `PerformAutoML` to `true` to have Amazon Forecast perform AutoML. This is a good option if you aren't sure which algorithm is suitable for your training data. In this case, `PerformHPO` must be false.
L253: 
L254: Type: Boolean
L255: 
L256: Required: No
L257: cite1†PerformHPO L258: 
L259: 
L260: Whether to perform hyperparameter optimization (HPO). HPO finds optimal hyperparameter values for your training data. The process of performing HPO is known as running a hyperparameter tuning job.
L261: 
L262: The default value is `false`. In this case, Amazon Forecast uses default hyperparameter values from the chosen algorithm.
L263: To override the default values, set `PerformHPO` to `true` and, optionally, supply the cite66†HyperParameterTuningJobConfig object.
