Testing models with production variants - Amazon SageMaker AI (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/model-ab-testing.html)
citeturn28view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 2 weeks ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/model-ab-testing.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 210
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Testing models with production variants - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Test models by specifying traffic distribution cite2†Test models by invoking specific variants cite3†Model A/B test example L5: # Testing models with production variants
L6: 
L7: In production ML workflows, data scientists and engineers frequently try to improve performance using various methods, such as cite4†Automatic model tuning with SageMaker AI , training on additional or more-recent data, improving feature selection, using better updated instances and serving containers. You can use production variants to compare your models, instances and containers, and choose the best performing candidate to respond to inference requests.
L8: With SageMaker AI multi-variant endpoints you can distribute endpoint invocation requests across multiple production variants by providing the traffic distribution for each variant, or you can invoke a specific variant directly for each request. In this topic, we look at both methods for testing ML models.
L9: ###### Topics
L10: 
L11:   * cite1†Test models by specifying traffic distribution L12: 
L13:   * cite2†Test models by invoking specific variants L14: 
L15:   * cite3†Model A/B test example L16: ## Test models by specifying traffic distribution
L17: 
L18: To test multiple models by distributing traffic between them, specify the percentage of the traffic that gets routed to each model by specifying the weight for each production variant in the endpoint configuration. For information, see cite5†CreateEndpointConfig . The following diagram shows how this works in more detail.
L19: 
L20: cite6†Image: Example showing how distributing traffic between models using InvokeEndpoint works in SageMaker AI. L21: ## Test models by invoking specific variants
L22: To test multiple models by invoking specific models for each request, specify the specific version of the model you want to invoke by providing a value for the `TargetVariant` parameter when you call cite7†InvokeEndpoint . SageMaker AI ensures that the request is processed by the production variant you specify. If you have already provided traffic distribution and specify a value for the `TargetVariant` parameter, the targeted routing overrides the random traffic distribution.
L23: The following diagram shows how this works in more detail.
L24: cite8†Image: Example showing how invoking specific models for each request using InvokeEndpoint works in SageMaker AI. L25: ## Model A/B test example
L26: 
L27: Performing A/B testing between a new model and an old model with production traffic can be an effective final step in the validation process for a new model. In A/B testing, you test different variants of your models and compare how each variant performs. If the newer version of the model delivers better performance than the previously existing version, replace the old version of the model with the new version in production.
L28: The following example shows how to perform A/B model testing. For a sample notebook that implements this example, see cite9†"A/B Testing ML models in production†sagemaker-examples.readthedocs.io .
L29: ### Step 1: Create and deploy models
L30: 
L31: First, we define where our models are located in Amazon S3. These locations are used when we deploy our models in subsequent steps:
L32: 
L33:     `model_url = f"s3://{path_to_model_1}"
L34:     model_url2 = f"s3://{path_to_model_2}"
L35:                 `
L36: Next, we create the model objects with the image and model data. These model objects are used to deploy production variants on an endpoint. The models are developed by training ML models on different data sets, different algorithms or ML frameworks, and different hyperparameters:
L37: 
L38:     `from sagemaker.core import image_uris
L39: 
L40:     model_name = f"DEMO-xgb-churn-pred-{datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S}"
L41:     model_name2 = f"DEMO-xgb-churn-pred2-{datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S}"
L42:     image_uri = get_image_uri(boto3.Session().region_name, 'xgboost', '0.90-1')
L43:     image_uri2 = get_image_uri(boto3.Session().region_name, 'xgboost', '0.90-2')
L44: 
L45:     sm_session.create_model(
L46:         name=model_name,
L47:         role=role,
L48:         container_defs={
L49:             'Image': image_uri,
L50:             'ModelDataUrl': model_url
L51:         }
L52:     )
L53: 
L54:     sm_session.create_model(
L55:         name=model_name2,
L56:         role=role,
L57:         container_defs={
L58:             'Image': image_uri2,
L59:             'ModelDataUrl': model_url2
L60:         }
L61:     )
L62:                 `
L63: We now create two production variants, each with its own different model and resource requirements (instance type and counts). This enables you to also test models on different instance types.
L64: We set an initial_weight of 1 for both variants. This means that 50% of requests go to `Variant1`, and the remaining 50% of requests to `Variant2`. The sum of weights across both variants is 2 and each variant has weight assignment of 1. This means that each variant receives 1/2, or 50%, of the total traffic.
L65: 
L66:     `from sagemaker.session import production_variant
L67: 
L68:     variant1 = production_variant(
L69:                    model_name=model_name,
L70:                    instance_type="ml.m5.xlarge",
L71:                    initial_instance_count=1,
L72:                    variant_name='Variant1',
L73:                    initial_weight=1,
L74:                )
L75: 
L76:     variant2 = production_variant(
L77:                    model_name=model_name2,
L78:                    instance_type="ml.m5.xlarge",
L79:                    initial_instance_count=1,
L80:                    variant_name='Variant2',
L81:                    initial_weight=1,
L82:                )
L83:                 `
L84: Finally we’re ready to deploy these production variants on a SageMaker AI endpoint.
L85: 
L86:     `endpoint_name = f"DEMO-xgb-churn-pred-{datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S}"
L87:     print(f"EndpointName={endpoint_name}")
L88: 
L89:     sm_session.endpoint_from_production_variants(
L90:         name=endpoint_name,
L91:         production_variants=[variant1, variant2]
L92:     )
L93:                 `
L94: ### Step 2: Invoke the deployed models
L95: 
L96: Now we send requests to this endpoint to get inferences in real time. We use both traffic distribution and direct targeting.
L97: First, we use traffic distribution that we configured in the previous step. Each inference response contains the name of the production variant that processes the request, so we can see that traffic to the two production variants is roughly equal.
L98: 
L99:     `# get a subset of test data for a quick test
L100:     !tail -120 test_data/test-dataset-input-cols.csv > test_data/test_sample_tail_input_cols.csv
L101:     print(f"Sending test traffic to the endpoint {endpoint_name}. \nPlease wait...")
L102:     with open('test_data/test_sample_tail_input_cols.csv', 'r') as f:
L103:         for row in f:
L104:             print(".", end="", flush=True)
L105:             payload = row.rstrip('\n')
L106:             sm_runtime.invoke_endpoint(
L107:                 EndpointName=endpoint_name,
L108:                 ContentType="text/csv",
L109:                 Body=payload
L110:             )
L111:             time.sleep(0.5)
L112: 
L113:     print("Done!")
L114:                 `
L115: SageMaker AI emits metrics such as `Latency` and `Invocations` for each variant in Amazon CloudWatch. For a complete list of metrics that SageMaker AI emits, see cite10†Amazon SageMaker AI metrics in Amazon CloudWatch . Let’s query CloudWatch to get the number of invocations per variant, to show how invocations are split across variants by default:
L116: 
L117: cite11†Image: Example CloudWatch number of invocations per variant. L118: Now let's invoke a specific version of the model by specifying `Variant1` as the `TargetVariant` in the call to `invoke_endpoint`.
L119: 
L120:     `print(f"Sending test traffic to the endpoint {endpoint_name}. \nPlease wait...")
L121:     with open('test_data/test_sample_tail_input_cols.csv', 'r') as f:
L122:         for row in f:
L123:             print(".", end="", flush=True)
L124:             payload = row.rstrip('\n')
L125:             sm_runtime.invoke_endpoint(
L126:                 EndpointName=endpoint_name,
L127:                 ContentType="text/csv",
L128:                 Body=payload,
L129:                 TargetVariant="Variant1"
L130:             )
L131:             time.sleep(0.5)
L132:                 `
L133: To confirm that all new invocations were processed by `Variant1`, we can query CloudWatch to get the number of invocations per variant. We see that for the most recent invocations (latest timestamp), all requests were processed by `Variant1`, as we had specified. There were no invocations made for `Variant2`.
L134: 
L135: cite12†Image: Example CloudWatch number of invocations for each variant. L136: ### Step 3: Evaluate model performance
L137: 
L138: To see which model version performs better, let's evaluate the accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and Receiver operating charactersistic/Area under the curve for each variant. First, let's look at these metrics for `Variant1`:
L139: 
L140: cite13†Image: Example receiver operating characteristic curve for Variant1. L141: 
L142: Now let's look at the metrics for `Variant2`:
L143: 
L144: cite14†Image: Example receiver operating characteristic curve for Variant2. L145: For most of our defined metrics, `Variant2` is performing better, so this is the one that we want to use in production.
L146: ### Step 4: Increase traffic to the best model
L147: Now that we have determined that `Variant2` performs better than `Variant1`, we shift more traffic to it. We can continue to use `TargetVariant` to invoke a specific model variant, but a simpler approach is to update the weights assigned to each variant by calling cite15†UpdateEndpointWeightsAndCapacities . This changes the traffic distribution to your production variants without requiring updates to your endpoint. Recall from the setup section that we set variant weights to split traffic 50/50.
L148: The CloudWatch metrics for the total invocations for each variant below show us the invocation patterns for each variant:
L149: cite16†Image: Example CloudWatch metrics for the total invocations for each variant. L150: Now we shift 75% of the traffic to `Variant2` by assigning new weights to each variant using `UpdateEndpointWeightsAndCapacities`. SageMaker AI now sends 75% of the inference requests to `Variant2` and remaining 25% of requests to `Variant1`.
L151: 
L152:     `sm.update_endpoint_weights_and_capacities(
L153:         EndpointName=endpoint_name,
L154:         DesiredWeightsAndCapacities=[
L155:             {
L156:                 "DesiredWeight": 25,
L157:                 "VariantName": variant1["VariantName"]
L158:             },
L159:             {
L160:                 "DesiredWeight": 75,
L161:                 "VariantName": variant2["VariantName"]
L162:             }
L163:         ]
L164:     )
L165:                 `
L166: The CloudWatch metrics for total invocations for each variant shows us higher invocations for `Variant2` than for `Variant1`:
L167: 
L168: cite17†Image: Example CloudWatch metrics for total invocations for each variant. L169: We can continue to monitor our metrics, and when we're satisfied with a variant's performance, we can route 100% of the traffic to that variant. We use cite15†`UpdateEndpointWeightsAndCapacities` to update the traffic assignments for the variants. The weight for `Variant1` is set to 0 and the weight for `Variant2` is set to 1. SageMaker AI now sends 100% of all inference requests to `Variant2`.
L170: 
L171:     `sm.update_endpoint_weights_and_capacities(
L172:         EndpointName=endpoint_name,
L173:         DesiredWeightsAndCapacities=[
L174:             {
L175:                 "DesiredWeight": 0,
L176:                 "VariantName": variant1["VariantName"]
L177:             },
L178:             {
L179:                 "DesiredWeight": 1,
L180:                 "VariantName": variant2["VariantName"]
L181:             }
L182:         ]
L183:     )
L184:                 `
L185: The CloudWatch metrics for the total invocations for each variant show that all inference requests are being processed by `Variant2` and there are no inference requests processed by `Variant1`.
L186: 
L187: cite18†Image: Example CloudWatch metrics for the total invocations for each variant. L188: 
L189: You can now safely update your endpoint and delete `Variant1` from your endpoint. You can also continue testing new models in production by adding new variants to your endpoint and following steps 2 - 4.

L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: How to use SageMaker AI execution roles - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: cite1†Create execution role cite2†Get your execution role cite3†Change your execution role cite4†Modify permissions to execution role cite5†Passing Roles cite6†CreateAutoMLJob and CreateAutoMLJobV2 API: Execution Role Permissions cite7†CreateDomain API: Execution Role Permissions cite8†CreateImage and UpdateImage APIs: Execution Role Permissions cite9†CreateNotebookInstance API: Execution Role Permissions cite10†CreateHyperParameterTuningJob API: Execution Role Permissions cite11†CreateProcessingJob API: Execution Role Permissions cite12†CreateTrainingJob API: Execution Role Permissions cite13†CreateModel API: Execution Role Permissions L4: # How to use SageMaker AI execution roles
L5: 
L6: Amazon SageMaker AI performs operations on your behalf using other AWS services. You must grant SageMaker AI permissions to use these services and the resources they act upon. You grant SageMaker AI these permissions using an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role. For more information on IAM roles, see cite14†IAM roles .
L7: 
L8: To create and use an execution role, you can use the following procedures.
L9: ## Create execution role
L10: 
L11: Use the following procedure to create an execution role with the IAM managed policy, `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess`, attached. If your use case requires more granular permissions, use other sections on this page to create an execution role that meets your business needs. You can create an execution role using the SageMaker AI console or the AWS CLI.
L12: ###### Important
L13: 
L14: The IAM managed policy, `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess`, used in the following procedure only grants the execution role permission to perform certain Amazon S3 actions on buckets or objects with `SageMaker`, `Sagemaker`, `sagemaker`, or `aws-glue` in the name. To learn how to add an additional policy to an execution role to grant it access to other Amazon S3 buckets and objects, see cite15†Add Additional Amazon S3 Permissions to a SageMaker AI Execution Role .
L15: ###### Note
L16: 
L17: You can create an execution role directly when you create a SageMaker AI domain or a notebook instance.
L18: 
L19:   * For information on how to create a SageMaker AI domain, see cite16†Guide to getting set up with Amazon SageMaker AI .
L20: 
L21:   * For information on how to create a notebook instance, see cite17†Create an Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instance for the tutorial .
L22: 
L23: To create a new execution role from the SageMaker AI console
L24:   1. Open the IAM console at cite18†https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/†console.aws.amazon.com .
L25: 
L26:   2. Choose Roles and then choose Create role.
L27: 
L28:   3. Keep AWS service as the Trusted entity type and then use the down arrow to find SageMaker AI in Use cases for other AWS services.
L29: 
L30:   4. Choose SageMaker AI – Execution and then choose Next.
L31:   5. The IAM managed policy, `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess`, is automatically attached to the role. To see the permissions included in this policy, choose the plus (+) sign next to the policy name. Choose Next.
L32: 
L33:   6. Enter a Role name and a Description.
L34: 
L35:   7. (Optional) Add additional permissions and tags to the role.
L36: 
L37:   8. Choose Create role.
L38: 
L39:   9. On the Roles section of the IAM console, find the role you just created. If needed, use the text box to search for the role using the role name.
L40:   10. On the role summary page, make note of the ARN.
L41: 
L42: To create a new execution role from the AWS CLI
L43: 
L44: Before you create an execution role using the AWS CLI, make sure to update and configure it by following the instructions in cite19†(Optional) Configure the AWS CLI , then continue with the instructions in cite20†Custom setup using the AWS CLI .
L45: 
L46: Once you have created an execution role, you can associate it with a SageMaker AI domain, a user profile, or with a Jupyter notebook instance.
L47:   * To learn about how to associate an execution role with an existing SageMaker AI domain, see cite21†Edit domain settings .
L48: 
L49:   * To learn about how to associate an execution role with an existing user profile, see cite22†Add user profiles .
L50: 
L51:   * To learn about how to associate an execution role with an existing notebook instance, see cite23†Update a Notebook Instance .
L52: You can also pass the ARN of an execution role to your API call. For example, using cite24†Amazon SageMaker Python SDK†sagemaker.readthedocs.io , you can pass the ARN of your execution role to a ModelTrainer. In the code sample that follows, we create a ModelTrainer using the XGBoost algorithm container and pass the ARN of the execution role as a parameter. For the full example on GitHub, see cite25†Customer Churn Prediction with XGBoost†github.com .

L80: ### Add Additional Amazon S3 Permissions to a SageMaker AI Execution Role
L81: 
L82: When you use a SageMaker AI feature with resources in Amazon S3, such as input data, the execution role you specify in your request (for example `CreateTrainingJob`) is used to access these resources.
L83: If you attach the IAM managed policy, `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess`, to an execution role, that role has permission to perform certain Amazon S3 actions on buckets or objects with `SageMaker`, `Sagemaker`, `sagemaker`, or `aws-glue` in the name. It also has permission to perform the following actions on any Amazon S3 resource:
L84: 
L85:     `"s3:CreateBucket",
L86:     "s3:GetBucketLocation",
L87:     "s3:ListBucket",
L88:     "s3:ListAllMyBuckets",
L89:     "s3:GetBucketCors",
L90:     "s3:PutBucketCors"`
L91: To give an execution role permissions to access one or more specific buckets in Amazon S3, you can attach a policy similar to the following to the role. This policy grants an IAM role permission to perform all actions that `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess` allows but restricts this access to the buckets amzn-s3-demo-bucket1 and amzn-s3-demo-bucket2. Refer to the security documentation for the specific SageMaker AI feature you are using to learn more about the Amazon S3 permissions required for that feature.
L92: JSON
L93: 
L94: 
L95:     ``{
L96:         "Version":"2012-10-17",
L97:         "Statement": [
L98:             {
L99:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L100:                 "Action": [
L101:                     "s3:GetObject",
L102:                     "s3:PutObject",
L103:                     "s3:DeleteObject",
L104:                     "s3:AbortMultipartUpload"
L105:                 ],
L106:                 "Resource": [
L107:                     "arn:aws:s3:::`amzn-s3-demo-bucket1/*`",
L108:                     "arn:aws:s3:::`amzn-s3-demo-bucket2/*`"
L109:                 ]
L110:             },
L111:             {
L112:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L113:                 "Action": [
L114:                     "s3:CreateBucket",
L115:                     "s3:GetBucketLocation",
L116:                     "s3:ListBucket",
L117:                     "s3:ListAllMyBuckets",
L118:                     "s3:GetBucketCors",
L119:                     "s3:PutBucketCors"
L120:                 ],
L121:                 "Resource": "*"
L122:             },
L123:             {
L124:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L125:                 "Action": [
L126:                     "s3:GetBucketAcl",
L127:                     "s3:PutObjectAcl"
L128:                 ],
L129:                 "Resource": [
L130:                     "arn:aws:s3:::`amzn-s3-demo-bucket1`",
L131:                     "arn:aws:s3:::`amzn-s3-demo-bucket2`"
L132:                 ]
L133:             }
L134:         ]
L135:     }`

L215: ## Change your execution role
L216: 
L217: An execution role is an IAM role that a SageMaker AI identity (like a SageMaker AI user, space, or domain) assumes. Changing the IAM role changes the permissions for all of the identities assuming that role.
L218: 
L219: When you change an execution role the corresponding space's execution role will also change. The effects of the change may take some time to propagate.
L220:   * When you change a user's execution role, the private spaces created by that user will assume the changed execution role.
L221: 
L222:   * When you change a space's default execution role, the shared spaces in the domain will assume the changed execution role.
L223: 
L224: For more information on execution roles and spaces, see cite35†Understanding domain space permissions and execution roles .
L225: 
L226: You can change the execution role for a identity to a different IAM role by using one of the following instructions.
L227: If, instead, you want to modify a role that an identity is assuming, see cite4†Modify permissions to execution role .

L299: ## Modify permissions to execution role
L300: 
L301: You can modify existing permissions to the execution role of an identity (like a SageMaker AI user, space, or domain). This is done by finding the appropriate IAM role that the identity is assuming, then modifying that IAM role. The following will provide instructions on achieving this through the console.
L302: 
L303: When you modify an execution role the corresponding space's execution role will also change. The effects of the change may not be immediate.
L304:   * When you modify a user's execution role, the private spaces created by that user will assume the modified execution role.
L305: 
L306:   * When you modify a space's default execution role, the shared spaces in the domain will assume the modified execution role.
L307:

L309: 
L310: If, instead, you want to change a role that an identity is assuming, see cite3†Change your execution role .
L311: ###### To modify permissions to your execution roles
L312: 
L313:   1. First get name of the identity you would like to modify.
L314: 
L315:      * cite28†Get domain execution role L316: 
L317:      * cite29†Get space execution role L318: 
L319:      * cite30†Get user execution role L320:

L323: ## Passing Roles
L324: 
L325: Actions like passing a role between services are a common function within SageMaker AI. You can find more details on cite41†Actions, Resources, and Condition Keys for SageMaker AI in the Service Authorization Reference.
L326: You pass the role (`iam:PassRole`) when making these API calls: cite42†`CreateAutoMLJob` , cite43†`CreateCompilationJob` , cite44†`CreateDomain` , cite45†`CreateFeatureGroup` , cite46†`CreateFlowDefiniton` , cite47†`CreateHyperParameterTuningJob` , cite48†`CreateImage` , cite49†`CreateLabelingJob` , cite50†`CreateModel` , cite51†`CreateMonitoringSchedule` , cite52†`CreateNotebookInstance` , cite53†`CreateProcessingJob` , cite54†`CreateTrainingJob` , cite55†`CreateUserProfile` , cite56†`RenderUiTemplate` , cite57†`UpdateImage` , and cite58†`UpdateNotebookInstance` .
L327: You attach the following trust policy to the IAM role which grants SageMaker AI principal permissions to assume the role, and is the same for all of the execution roles:
L328: 
L329: JSON
L330: 
L331: 
L332: 
L333: 
L334:     ``{
L335:         "Version":"2012-10-17",
L336:         "Statement": [
L337:             {
L338:                 "Effect": "Allow",
L339:                 "Principal": {
L340:                     "Service": "sagemaker.amazonaws.com"
L341:                 },
L342:                 "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
L343:             }
L344:         ]
L345:     }`
L346:     `
L347: The permissions that you need to grant to the role vary depending on the API that you call. The following sections explain these permissions.
L348: ###### Note
L349: Instead of managing permissions by crafting a permission policy, you can use the AWS-managed `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess` permission policy. The permissions in this policy are fairly broad, to allow for any actions you might want to perform in SageMaker AI. For a listing of the policy including information about the reasons for adding many of the permissions, see cite59†AWS managed policy: AmazonSageMakerFullAccess .
L350: If you prefer to create custom policies and manage permissions to scope the permissions only to the actions you need to perform with the execution role, see the following topics.
L351: ###### Important
L352: 
L353: If you're running into issues, see cite60†Troubleshooting Amazon SageMaker AI Identity and Access .
L354: 
L355: For more information about IAM roles, see cite61†IAM Roles in the Service Authorization Reference.

L6: # Data Transformations Reference
L7: ###### Topics
L8: 
L9:   * cite1†N-gram Transformation L10: 
L11:   * cite2†Orthogonal Sparse Bigram (OSB) Transformation L12:

L21:   * cite7†Cartesian Product Transformation L22: ## N-gram Transformation
L23: 
L24: The n-gram transformation takes a text variable as input and produces strings corresponding to sliding a window of (user-configurable) n words, generating outputs in the process. For example, consider the text string "I really enjoyed reading this book".
L25: 
L26: Specifying the n-gram transformation with window size=1 simply gives you all the individual words in that string:
L27: 
L28:     `
L29:     {"I", "really", "enjoyed", "reading", "this", "book"}
L30:     `
L31: Specifying the n-gram transformation with window size =2 gives you all the two-word combinations as well as the one-word combinations:
L32: 
L33:     `
L34:     {"I really", "really enjoyed", "enjoyed reading", "reading this", "this
L35:     book", "I", "really", "enjoyed", "reading", "this", "book"}
L36:     `
L37: Specifying the n-gram transformation with window size = 3 will add the three-word combinations to this list, yielding the following:
L38: 
L39:     `
L40:     {"I really enjoyed", "really enjoyed reading", "enjoyed reading this",
L41:     "reading this book", "I really", "really enjoyed", "enjoyed reading",
L42:     "reading this", "this book", "I", "really", "enjoyed", "reading",
L43:     "this", "book"}
L44:     `
L45: You can request n-grams with a size ranging from 2-10 words. N-grams with size 1 are generated implicitly for all inputs whose type is marked as text in the data schema, so you do not have to ask for them. Finally, keep in mind that n-grams are generated by breaking the input data on whitespace characters.
L46: That means that, for example, punctuation characters will be considered a part of the word tokens: generating n-grams with a window of 2 for string "red, green, blue" will yield {"red,", "green,", "blue,", "red, green", "green, blue"}. You can use the punctuation remover processor (described later in this document) to remove the punctuation symbols if this is not what you want.
L47: To compute n-grams of window size 3 for variable var1:
L48: 
L49:     `
L50:     "ngram(var1, 3)"
L51:     `
L52: ## Orthogonal Sparse Bigram (OSB) Transformation
L53: 
L54: The OSB transformation is intended to aid in text string analysis and is an alternative to the bi-gram transformation (n-gram with window size 2). OSBs are generated by sliding the window of size n over the text, and outputting every pair of words that includes the first word in the window.
L55: To build each OSB, its constituent words are joined by the "_" (underscore) character, and every skipped token is indicated by adding another underscore into the OSB. Thus, the OSB encodes not just the tokens seen within a window, but also an indication of number of tokens skipped within that same window.
L56: To illustrate, consider the string "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog", and OSBs of size 4. The six four-word windows, and the last two shorter windows from the end of the string are shown in the following example, as well OSBs generated from each:
L57: Window, {OSBs generated}
L58: 
L59:     `
L60:     "The quick brown fox", {The_quick, The__brown, The___fox}
L61: 
L62:     "quick brown fox jumps", {quick_brown, quick__fox, quick___jumps}
L63: 
L64:     "brown fox jumps over", {brown_fox, brown__jumps, brown___over}
L65: 
L66:     "fox jumps over the", {fox_jumps, fox__over, fox___the}
L67: 
L68:     "jumps over the lazy", {jumps_over, jumps__the, jumps___lazy}
L69: 
L70:     "over the lazy dog", {over_the, over__lazy, over___dog}
L71: 
L72:     "the lazy dog", {the_lazy, the__dog}
L73:     "lazy dog", {lazy_dog}
L74:     `
L75: Orthogonal sparse bigrams are an alternative for n-grams that might work better in some situations. If your data has large text fields (10 or more words), experiment to see which works better. Note that what constitutes a large text field may vary depending on the situation. However, with larger text fields, OSBs have been empirically shown to uniquely represent the text due to the special skip symbol (the underscore).
L76: You can request a window size of 2 to 10 for OSB transformations on input text variables.
L77: 
L78: To compute OSBs with window size 5 for variable var1:
L79: 
L80: "osb(var1, 5)"
L81: ## Lowercase Transformation
L82: 
L83: The lowercase transformation processor converts text inputs to lowercase. For example, given the input "The Quick Brown Fox Jumps Over the Lazy Dog", the processor will output "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog".
L84: 
L85: To apply lowercase transformation to the variable var1:
L86: 
L87: "lowercase(var1)"
L88: ## Remove Punctuation Transformation
L89: Amazon ML implicitly splits inputs marked as text in the data schema on whitespace. Punctuation in the string ends up either adjoining word tokens, or as separate tokens entirely, depending on the whitespace surrounding it. If this is undesirable, the punctuation remover transformation may be used to remove punctuation symbols from generated features. For example, given the string "Welcome to AML - please fasten your seat-belts!", the following set of tokens is implicitly generated:
L90:     `{"Welcome", "to", "Amazon", "ML", "-", "please", "fasten", "your", "seat-belts!"}`
L91: Applying the punctuation remover processor to this string results in this set:
L92: 
L93:     `{"Welcome", "to", "Amazon", "ML", "please", "fasten", "your", "seat-belts"}`
L94: 
L95: Note that only the prefix and suffix punctuation marks are removed. Punctuations that appear in the middle of a token, e.g. the hyphen in "seat-belts", are not removed.
L96: 
L97: To apply punctuation removal to the variable var1:
L98: 
L99: "no_punct(var1)"
L100: ## Quantile Binning Transformation
L101: 
L102: The quantile binning processor takes two inputs, a numerical variable and a parameter called bin number, and outputs a categorical variable. The purpose is to discover non-linearity in the variable's distribution by grouping observed values together.
L103: In many cases, the relationship between a numeric variable and the target is not linear (the numeric variable value does not increase or decrease monotonically with the target). In such cases, it might be useful to bin the numeric feature into a categorical feature representing different ranges of the numeric feature. Each categorical feature value (bin) can then be modeled as having its own linear relationship with the target.
L104: For example, let's say you know that the continuous numeric feature account_age is not linearly correlated with likelihood to purchase a book. You can bin age into categorical features that might be able to capture the relationship with the target more accurately.
L105: The quantile binning processor can be used to instruct Amazon ML to establish n bins of equal size based on the distribution of all input values of the age variable, and then to substitute each number with a text token containing the bin. The optimum number of bins for a numeric variable is dependent on characteristics of the variable and its relationship to the target, and this is best determined through experimentation.
L106: Amazon ML suggests the optimal bin number for a numeric feature based on data statistics in the cite8†Suggested Recipe .
L107: You can request between 5 and 1000 quantile bins to be computed for any numeric input variable.
L108: 
L109: To following example shows how to compute and use 50 bins in place of numeric variable var1:
L110: 
L111: "quantile_bin(var1, 50)"
L112: ## Normalization Transformation
L113: 
L114: The normalization transformer normalizes numeric variables to have a mean of zero and variance of one. Normalization of numeric variables can help the learning process if there are very large range differences between numeric variables because variables with the highest magnitude could dominate the ML model, no matter if the feature is informative with respect to the target or not.
L115: 
L116: To apply this transformation to numeric variable var1, add this to the recipe:
L117: normalize(var1)
L118: 
L119: This transformer can also take a user defined group of numeric variables or the pre-defined group for all numeric variables (ALL_NUMERIC) as input:
L120: 
L121: normalize(ALL_NUMERIC)
L122: 
L123: Note
L124: 
L125: It is not mandatory to use the normalization processor for numeric variables.
L126: ## Cartesian Product Transformation
L127: The Cartesian transformation generates permutations of two or more text or categorical input variables. This transformation is used when an interaction between variables is suspected. For example, consider the bank marketing dataset that is used in Tutorial: Using Amazon ML to Predict Responses to a Marketing Offer. Using this dataset, we would like to predict whether a person would respond positively to a bank promotion, based on the economic and demographic information.
L128: We might suspect that the person's job type is somewhat important (perhaps there is a correlation between being employed in certain fields and having the money available), and the highest level of education attained is also important. We might also have a deeper intuition that there is a strong signal in the interaction of these two variables—for example, that the promotion is particularly well-suited to customers who are entrepreneurs who earned a university degree.
L129: The Cartesian product transformation takes categorical variables or text as input, and produces new features that capture the interaction between these input variables. Specifically, for each training example, it will create a combination of features, and add them as a standalone feature. For example, let's say our simplified input rows look like this:
L130: 
L131: target, education, job
L132: 
L133: 0, university.degree, technician
L134: 
L135: 0, high.school, services
L136: 
L137: 1, university.degree, admin
L138: If we specify that the Cartesian transformation is to be applied to the categorical variables education and job fields, the resultant feature education_job_interaction will look like this:
L139: 
L140: target, education_job_interaction
L141: 
L142: 0, university.degree_technician
L143: 
L144: 0, high.school_services
L145: 
L146: 1, university.degree_admin
L147: The Cartesian transformation is even more powerful when it comes to working on sequences of tokens, as is the case when one of its arguments is a text variable that is implicitly or explicitly split into tokens. For example, consider the task of classifying a book as being a textbook or not.
L148: Intuitively, we might think that there is something about the book's title that can tell us it is a textbook (certain words might occur more frequently in textbooks' titles), and we might also think that there is something about the book's binding that is predictive (textbooks are more likely to be hardcover), but it's really the combination of some words in the title and binding that is most predictive.
L149: For a real-world example, the following table shows the results of applying the Cartesian processor to the input variables binding and title:
L150: Textbook  | Title  | Binding  | Cartesian product of no_punct(Title) and Binding
L151: --- | --- | --- | ---
L152: 1  | Economics: Principles, Problems, Policies  | Hardcover  | {"Economics_Hardcover", "Principles_Hardcover", "Problems_Hardcover", "Policies_Hardcover"}
L153: 0  | The Invisible Heart: An Economics Romance  | Softcover  | {"The_Softcover", "Invisible_Softcover", "Heart_Softcover", "An_Softcover", "Economics_Softcover", "Romance_Softcover"}
L154: 0  | Fun With Problems  | Softcover  | {"Fun_Softcover", "With_Softcover", "Problems_Softcover"}
L155: The following example shows how to apply the Cartesian transformer to var1 and var2:
L156: 
L157: cartesian(var1, var2)
L158:

Controlling access from VPC endpoints with bucket policies - Amazon Simple Storage Service (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies-vpc-endpoint.html)
citeturn33view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies-vpc-endpoint.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 135
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Controlling access from VPC endpoints with bucket policies - Amazon Simple Storage Service
L3: 
L4: cite1†Restricting access to a specific VPC endpoint cite2†Restricting access to a specific VPC cite3†Restricting access to an IPv6 VPC endpoint L5: # Controlling access from VPC endpoints with bucket policies
L6: 
L7: You can use Amazon S3 bucket policies to control access to buckets from specific virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints or specific VPCs. This section contains example bucket policies that you can use to control Amazon S3 bucket access from VPC endpoints. To learn how to set up VPC endpoints, see cite4†VPC Endpoints in the VPC User Guide.
L8: A VPC enables you to launch AWS resources into a virtual network that you define. A VPC endpoint enables you to create a private connection between your VPC and another AWS service. This private connection doesn't require access over the internet, through a virtual private network (VPN) connection, through a NAT instance, or through Direct Connect.
L9: A VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 is a logical entity within a VPC that allows connectivity only to Amazon S3. The VPC endpoint routes requests to Amazon S3 and routes responses back to the VPC. VPC endpoints change only how requests are routed. Amazon S3 public endpoints and DNS names will continue to work with VPC endpoints. For important information about using VPC endpoints with Amazon S3, see cite5†Gateway endpoints and cite6†Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3 in the VPC User Guide.
L10: VPC endpoints for Amazon S3 provide two ways to control access to your Amazon S3 data:
L11: 
L12:   * You can control the requests, users, or groups that are allowed through a specific VPC endpoint. For information about this type of access control, see cite7†Controlling access to VPC endpoints using endpoint policies in the VPC User Guide.
L13:   * You can control which VPCs or VPC endpoints have access to your buckets by using Amazon S3 bucket policies. For examples of this type of bucket policy access control, see the following topics on restricting access.
L14: ###### Topics
L15: 
L16:   * cite1†Restricting access to a specific VPC endpoint L17: 
L18:   * cite2†Restricting access to a specific VPC L19: 
L20:   * cite3†Restricting access to an IPv6 VPC endpoint L21: ###### Important
L22: 
L23: When applying the Amazon S3 bucket policies for VPC endpoints described in this section, you might block your access to the bucket unintentionally. Bucket permissions that are intended to specifically limit bucket access to connections originating from your VPC endpoint can block all connections to the bucket. For information about how to fix this issue, see cite8†How do I fix my bucket policy when it has the wrong VPC or VPC endpoint ID?†aws.amazon.com in the AWS Support Knowledge Center.
L24: ## Restricting access to a specific VPC endpoint
L25: The following is an example of an Amazon S3 bucket policy that restricts access to a specific bucket, `amzn-s3-demo-bucket`, only from the VPC endpoint with the ID `vpce-0abcdef1234567890`. If the specified endpoint is not used, the policy denies all access to the bucket. The `aws:SourceVpce` condition specifies the endpoint. The `aws:SourceVpce` condition doesn't require an Amazon Resource Name (ARN) for the VPC endpoint resource, only the VPC endpoint ID.
L26: For more information about using conditions in a policy, see cite9†Bucket policy examples using condition keys .
L27: ###### Important
L28: 
L29:   * Before using the following example policy, replace the VPC endpoint ID with an appropriate value for your use case. Otherwise, you won't be able to access your bucket.
L30: 
L31:   * This policy disables console access to the specified bucket because console requests don't originate from the specified VPC endpoint.
L32: 
L33: JSON
L34: 
L35: 
L36:     ``{
L37:        "Version":"2012-10-17",
L38:        "Id": "Policy1415115909152",
L39:        "Statement": [
L40:          {
L41:            "Sid": "Access-to-specific-VPCE-only",
L42:            "Principal": "*",
L43:            "Action": "s3:*",
L44:            "Effect": "Deny",
L45:            "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::`amzn-s3-demo-bucket`",
L46:                         "arn:aws:s3:::`amzn-s3-demo-bucket`/*"],
L47:            "Condition": {
L48:              "StringNotEquals": {
L49:                "aws:SourceVpce": "`vpce-0abcdef1234567890`"
L50:              }
L51:            }
L52:          }
L53:        ]
L54:     }`
L55:     `
L56: ## Restricting access to a specific VPC
L57: You can create a bucket policy that restricts access to a specific VPC by using the `aws:SourceVpc` condition. This is useful if you have multiple VPC endpoints configured in the same VPC, and you want to manage access to your Amazon S3 buckets for all of your endpoints. The following is an example of a policy that denies access to `amzn-s3-demo-bucket` and its objects from anyone outside VPC `vpc-1a2b3c4d`. If the specified VPC isn't used, the policy denies all access to the bucket.
L58: This statement doesn't grant access to the bucket. To grant access, you must add a separate `Allow` statement. The `vpc-1a2b3c4d` condition key doesn't require an ARN for the VPC resource, only the VPC ID.
L59: ###### Important
L60: 
L61:   * Before using the following example policy, replace the VPC ID with an appropriate value for your use case. Otherwise, you won't be able to access your bucket.
L62: 
L63:   * This policy disables console access to the specified bucket because console requests don't originate from the specified VPC.
L64: 
L65: JSON
L66: 
L67: 
L68:     ``{
L69:        "Version":"2012-10-17",
L70:        "Id": "Policy1415115909153",
L71:        "Statement": [
L72:          {
L73:            "Sid": "Access-to-specific-VPC-only",
L74:            "Principal": "*",
L75:            "Action": "s3:*",
L76:            "Effect": "Deny",
L77:            "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket",
L78:                         "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"],
L79:            "Condition": {
L80:              "StringNotEquals": {
L81:                "aws:SourceVpc": "vpc-1a2b3c4d"
L82:              }
L83:            }
L84:          }
L85:        ]
L86:     }`
L87:     `
L88: ## Restricting access to an IPv6 VPC endpoint
L89: The following example policy denies all Amazon S3 (`s3:`) actions on the `amzn-s3-demo-bucket` bucket and its objects, unless the request originates from the specified VPC endpoint (`vpce-0a1b2c3d4e5f6g`) and the source IP address matches the provided IPv6 CIDR block.
L90: 
L91:     `{
L92:        "Version": "2012-10-17",
L93:        "Id": "Policy1415115909154",
L94:        "Statement": [
L95:          {
L96:            "Sid": "AccessSpecificIPv6VPCEOnly",
L97:            "Action": "s3:*",
L98:            "Effect": "Deny",
L99:            "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::``amzn-s3-demo-bucket``",
L100:                         "arn:aws:s3:::``amzn-s3-demo-bucket``/*"],
L101:            "Condition": {
L102:              "StringNotEquals": {
L103:                "aws:SourceVpce": "`vpce-0a1b2c3d4e5f6g`"
L104:              },
L105:             "NotIpAddress": {
L106:               "aws:VpcSourceIp": "2001:db8::/32"
L107:             }
L108:            }
L109:          }
L110:        ]
L111:     }
L112:     `
L113: For information on how to restrict access to your bucket based on specific IPs or VPCs, see cite10†How do I allow only specific VPC endpoints or IP addresses to access my Amazon S3 bucket?†repost.aws in the AWS re:Post Knowledge Center.

L2: How Amazon SageMaker AI Runs Your Training Image - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Run a training job with an entrypoint script bundled inside the Docker container cite2†Run a training job with an entrypoint script outside the Docker container L5: # How Amazon SageMaker AI Runs Your Training Image
L6: 
L7: You can use a custom entrypoint script to automate infrastructure to train in a production environment. If you pass your entrypoint script into your Docker container, you can also run it as a standalone script without rebuilding your images. SageMaker AI processes your training image using a Docker container entrypoint script.
L8: This section shows you how to use a custom entrypoint without using the training toolkit. If you want to use a custom entrypoint but are unfamiliar with how to manually configure a Docker container, we recommend that you use the cite3†SageMaker training toolkit library†github.com instead. For more information about how to use the training toolkit, see cite4†Adapting your own training container .
L9: By default, SageMaker AI looks for a script called `train` inside your container. You can also manually provide your own custom entrypoint by using the `ContainerArguments` and `ContainerEntrypoint` parameters of the cite5†AlgorithmSpecification API.
L10: 
L11: You have the following two options to manually configure your Docker container to run your image.
L12: 
L13:   * Use the cite6†CreateTrainingJob API and a Docker container with an entrypoint instruction contained inside of it.
L14:   * Use the `CreateTrainingJob` API, and pass your training script from outside of your Docker container.
L15: 
L16: If you pass your training script from outside your Docker container, you don't need to rebuild the Docker container when you update your script. You can also use several different scripts to run in the same container.
L17: Your entrypoint script should contain training code for your image. If you use the optional `source_dir` parameter inside an cite7†ModelTrainer†sagemaker.readthedocs.io , it should reference the relative Amazon S3 path to the folder containing your entrypoint script. You can reference multiple files using the `source_dir` parameter. If you do not use `source_dir`, you can specify the entrypoint using the `entry_point` parameter.
L18: For an example of a custom entrypoint script that contains a ModelTrainer, see cite8†Bring Your Own Model with SageMaker AI Script Mode†sagemaker-examples.readthedocs.io .
L19: SageMaker AI model training supports high-performance S3 Express One Zone directory buckets as a data input location for file mode, fast file mode, and pipe mode. You can also use S3 Express One Zone directory buckets to store your training output. To use S3 Express One Zone, provide the URI of an S3 Express One Zone directory bucket instead of an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket.
L20: You can only encrypt your SageMaker AI output data in directory buckets with server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) is not currently supported for storing SageMaker AI output data in directory buckets. For more information, see cite9†S3 Express One Zone .
L21: ## Run a training job with an entrypoint script bundled inside the Docker container
L22: 
L23: SageMaker AI can run an entrypoint script bundled inside your Docker container.
L24: 
L25:   * By default, Amazon SageMaker AI runs the following container.
L26: 
L27:     `docker run `image` train`
L28:   * SageMaker AI overrides any default cite10†CMD†docs.docker.com statements in a container by specifying the `train` argument after the image name. In your Docker container, use the following `exec` form of the `ENTRYPOINT` instruction.
L29: 
L30:     `ENTRYPOINT ["`executable`", "`param1`", "`param2`", ...]`
L31: 
L32: The following example shows how to specify a python entrypoint instruction called `k-means-algorithm.py`.
L33: 
L34:     `ENTRYPOINT ["python", "k-means-algorithm.py"]`
L35: The `exec` form of the `ENTRYPOINT` instruction starts the executable directly, not as a child of `/bin/sh`. This enables it to receive signals like `SIGTERM` and `SIGKILL` from SageMaker APIs. The following conditions apply when using the SageMaker APIs.
L36: 
L37:     * The cite6†`CreateTrainingJob` API has a stopping condition that directs SageMaker AI to stop model training after a specific time.
L38:     * The following shows the cite11†`StopTrainingJob` API. This API issues the equivalent of the `docker stop`, with a 2-minute timeout command to gracefully stop the specified container.
L39: 
L40:         `docker stop -t 120`
L41: The command attempts to stop the running container by sending a `SIGTERM` signal. After the 2-minute timeout, the API sends `SIGKILL` and forcibly stops the containers. If the container handles the `SIGTERM` gracefully and exits within 120 seconds from receiving it, no `SIGKILL` is sent.
L42: 
L43: If you want access to the intermediate model artifacts after SageMaker AI stops the training, add code to handle saving artifacts in your `SIGTERM` handler.
L44:   * If you plan to use GPU devices for model training, make sure that your containers are `nvidia-docker` compatible. Include only the CUDA toolkit on containers; don't bundle NVIDIA drivers with the image. For more information about `nvidia-docker`, see cite12†NVIDIA/nvidia-docker†github.com .
L45: 
L46:   * You can't use the `tini` initializer as your entrypoint script in SageMaker AI containers because it gets confused by the `train` and `serve` arguments.
L47:   * `/opt/ml` and all subdirectories are reserved by SageMaker training. When building your algorithm’s Docker image, make sure that you don't place any data that's required by your algorithm in this directory. Because if you do, the data may no longer be visible during training.
L48: 
L49: To bundle your shell or Python scripts inside your Docker image, or to provide the script in an Amazon S3 bucket or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), continue to the following section.
L50: ### Bundle your shell script in a Docker container
L51: 
L52: If you want to bundle a custom shell script inside your Docker image, use the following steps.
L53:   1. Copy your shell script from your working directory to inside your Docker container. The following code snippet copies a custom entrypoint script `custom_entrypoint.sh` from the current working directory to a Docker container located in `mydir`. The following example assumes that the base Docker image has Python installed.
L54: 
L55:     `FROM `<base-docker-image>`:`<tag>`
L56: 
L57:     # Copy custom entrypoint from current dir to /mydir on container
L58:     COPY `./custom_entrypoint.sh /mydir/ ``
L59:   2. Build and push a Docker container to the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (cite13†Amazon ECR ) by following the instructions at cite14†Pushing a Docker image in the Amazon ECR User Guide.
L60:   3. Launch the training job by running the following AWS CLI command.
L61: 
L62:     `aws --region `<your-region>` sagemaker create-training-job \
L63:     --training-job-name `<your-training-job-name>` \
L64:     --role-arn `<your-execution-role-arn>` \
L65:     --algorithm-specification '{ \
L66:         "TrainingInputMode": "File", \
L67:         "TrainingImage": "`<your-ecr-image>`", \
L68:         "ContainerEntrypoint": ["`/bin/sh`"], \
L69:         "ContainerArguments": ["`/mydir/custom_entrypoint.sh`"]}' \
L70:     --output-data-config '{"S3OutputPath": "`s3://custom-entrypoint-output-bucket/`"}' \
L71:     --resource-config '{"VolumeSizeInGB":`10`,"InstanceCount":`1`,"InstanceType":"`ml.m5.2xlarge`"}' \
L72:     --stopping-condition '{"MaxRuntimeInSeconds": `180`}'                    `
L73: ### Bundle your Python script in a Docker container
L74: 
L75: To bundle a custom Python script inside your Docker image, use the following steps.
L76:   1. Copy your Python script from your working directory to inside your Docker container. The following code snippet copies a custom entrypoint script `custom_entrypoint.py` from the current working directory to a Docker container located in `mydir`.
L77: 
L78:     `FROM `<base-docker-image>`:`<tag>`
L79:     # Copy custom entrypoint from current dir to /mydir on container
L80:     COPY `./custom_entrypoint.py /mydir/``
L81:   2. Launch the training job by running the following AWS CLI command.
L82: 
L83:     `--algorithm-specification '{ \
L84:         "TrainingInputMode": "File", \
L85:         "TrainingImage": "`<your-ecr-image>`", \
L86:         "ContainerEntrypoint": ["`python`"], \
L87:         "ContainerArguments": ["`/mydir/custom_entrypoint.py`"]}' \`
L88: ## Run a training job with an entrypoint script outside the Docker container
L89: 
L90: You can use your own Docker container for training and pass in an entrypoint script from outside the Docker container. There are some benefits to structuring your entrypoint script outside the container. If you update your entrypoint script, you don't need to rebuild the Docker container. You can also use several different scripts to run in the same container.
L91: Specify the location of your training script using the `ContainerEntrypoint` and `ContainerArguments` parameters of the cite5†AlgorithmSpecification API. These entrypoints and arguments behave in the same manner as Docker entrypoints and arguments. The values in these parameters override the corresponding `ENTRYPOINT` or `CMD` provided as part of the Docker container.
L92: When you pass your custom entrypoint script to your Docker training container, the inputs that you provide determine the behavior of the container.
L93: 
L94:   * For example, if you provide only `ContainerEntrypoint`, the request syntax using the CreateTrainingJob API is as follows.
L95: 
L96:     `{
L97:         "AlgorithmSpecification": {
L98:             "ContainerEntrypoint": ["`string`"],
L99:             ...
L100:             }
L101:     }`
L102: Then, the SageMaker training backend runs your custom entrypoint as follows.
L103: 
L104:     `docker run --entrypoint `<ContainerEntrypoint>` image`
L105: ###### Note
L106: 
L107: If `ContainerEntrypoint` is provided, the SageMaker training backend runs the image with the given entrypoint and overrides the default `ENTRYPOINT` in the image.
L108: 
L109:   * If you provide only `ContainerArguments`, SageMaker AI assumes that the Docker container contains an entrypoint script. The request syntax using the `CreateTrainingJob` API is as follows.
L110: 
L111:     `{
L112:         "AlgorithmSpecification": {
L113:             "ContainerArguments": ["`arg1`", "`arg2`"],
L114:             ...
L115:         }
L116:     }`
L117: The SageMaker training backend runs your custom entrypoint as follows.
L118: 
L119:     `docker run image `<ContainerArguments>``
L120: 
L121:   * If your provide both the `ContainerEntrypoint` and `ContainerArguments`, then the request syntax using the `CreateTrainingJob` API is as follows.
L122: 
L123:     `{
L124:         "AlgorithmSpecification": {
L125:             "ContainerEntrypoint": ["`string`"],
L126:             "ContainerArguments": ["`arg1`", "`arg2`"],
L127:             ...
L128:         }
L129:     }                   `
L130: The SageMaker training backend runs your custom entrypoint as follows.
L131: 
L132:     `docker run --entrypoint `<ContainerEntrypoint>` image `<ContainerArguments>``
L133: 
L134: You can use any supported `InputDataConfig` source in the `CreateTrainingJob` API to provide an entrypoint script to run your training image.
L135: ### Provide your entrypoint script in an Amazon S3 bucket
L136: 
L137: To provide a custom entrypoint script using an S3 bucket, use the `S3DataSource` parameter of the cite15†DataSource API to specify the location of the script. If you use the `S3DataSource` parameter, the following are required.
L138: 
L139:   * The cite16†InputMode must be of the type `File`.
L140: 
L141:   * The cite15†S3DataDistributionType must be `FullyReplicated`.
L142: The following example has a script called custom_entrypoint.sh placed in a path to an S3 bucket `s3://<bucket-name>/<bucket prefix>/custom_entrypoint.sh`.
L143: 
L144:     `#!/bin/bash
L145:     echo "Running custom_entrypoint.sh"
L146:     echo "Hello you have provided the following arguments: " "$@"`
L147: 
L148: Next, you must set the configuration of the input data channel to run a training job. Do this either by using the AWS CLI directly or with a JSON file.
L149: #### Configure the input data channel using AWS CLI with a JSON file
L150: To configure your input data channel with a JSON file, use AWS CLI as shown in the following code structure. Ensure that all of the following fields use the request syntax defined in the cite17†CreateTrainingJob API.
L151: 
L152:     `// run-my-training-job.json
L153:     {
L154:      "cite18†AlgorithmSpecification ": {
L155:             "ContainerEntrypoint": ["`/bin/sh`"],
L156:             "ContainerArguments": ["/opt/ml/input/data/`<your_channel_name>`/`custom_entrypoint.sh`"],
L157:              ...
L158:        },
L159:       "cite19†InputDataConfig ": [
L160:         {
L161:             "cite20†ChannelName ": "`<your_channel_name>`",
L162:             "cite21†DataSource ": {
L163:                 "cite15†S3DataSource ": {
L164:                     "cite22†S3DataDistributionType ": "FullyReplicated",
L165:                     "cite23†S3DataType ": "S3Prefix",
L166:                     "cite24†S3Uri ": "s3://`<bucket-name>`/`<bucket_prefix>`"
L167:                 }
L168:             },
L169:             "cite16†InputMode ": "File",
L170:         },
L171:         ...]
L172:     }`
L173: Next, run the AWS CLI command to launch the training job from the JSON file as follows.
L174: 
L175:     `aws sagemaker create-training-job --cli-input-json file:`//run-my-training-job.json``
L176: #### Configure the input data channel using AWS CLI directly
L177: To configure your input data channel without a JSON file, use the following AWS CLI code structure.
L178: 
L179:     `aws --region `<your-region>` sagemaker create-training-job \
L180:     --training-job-name `<your-training-job-name>` \
L181:     --role-arn `<your-execution-role-arn>` \
L182:     --algorithm-specification '{ \
L183:         "TrainingInputMode": "File", \
L184:         "TrainingImage": "`<your-ecr-image>`", \
L185:         "ContainerEntrypoint": ["`/bin/sh`"], \
L186:         "ContainerArguments": ["`/opt/ml/input/data/<your_channel_name>/custom_entrypoint.sh"]}`' \
L187:     --input-data-config '[{ \
L188:         "ChannelName":"`<your_channel_name>`", \
L189:         "DataSource":{ \
L190:             "S3DataSource":{ \
L191:                 "S3DataType":"S3Prefix", \
L192:                 "S3Uri":"s3://`<bucket-name>`/`<bucket_prefix>`", \
L193:                 "S3DataDistributionType":"FullyReplicated"}}}]' \
L194:     --output-data-config '{"S3OutputPath": "`s3://custom-entrypoint-output-bucket/`"}' \
L195:     --resource-config '{"VolumeSizeInGB":`10`,"InstanceCount":`1`,"InstanceType":"`ml.m5.2xlarge`"}' \
L196:     --stopping-condition '{"MaxRuntimeInSeconds": `180`}'`

L2: Model Fit: Underfitting vs. Overfitting - Amazon Machine Learning
L3: # Model Fit: Underfitting vs. Overfitting
L4: 
L5: Understanding model fit is important for understanding the root cause for poor model accuracy. This understanding will guide you to take corrective steps. We can determine whether a predictive model is underfitting or overfitting the training data by looking at the prediction error on the training data and the evaluation data.
L6: 
L7: cite1†Image: Three graphs showing underfitting, balanced, and overfitting models with data points and trend lines. L8: Your model is underfitting the training data when the model performs poorly on the training data. This is because the model is unable to capture the relationship between the input examples (often called X) and the target values (often called Y). Your model is overfitting your training data when you see that the model performs well on the training data but does not perform well on the evaluation data.
L9: This is because the model is memorizing the data it has seen and is unable to generalize to unseen examples.
L10: Poor performance on the training data could be because the model is too simple (the input features are not expressive enough) to describe the target well. Performance can be improved by increasing model flexibility. To increase model flexibility, try the following:
L11: 
L12:   * Add new domain-specific features and more feature Cartesian products, and change the types of feature processing used (e.g., increasing n-grams size)
L13: 
L14:   * Decrease the amount of regularization used
L15: If your model is overfitting the training data, it makes sense to take actions that reduce model flexibility. To reduce model flexibility, try the following:
L16: 
L17:   * Feature selection: consider using fewer feature combinations, decrease n-grams size, and decrease the number of numeric attribute bins.
L18: 
L19:   * Increase the amount of regularization used.
L20: Accuracy on training and test data could be poor because the learning algorithm did not have enough data to learn from. You could improve performance by doing the following:
L21: 
L22:   * Increase the amount of training data examples.
L23: 
L24:   * Increase the number of passes on the existing training data.

citeturn36view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/machine-learning/latest/dg/training-parameters1.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 51

L3: 
L4: cite1†Learning Rate cite2†Model Size cite3†Number of Passes cite4†Data Shuffling cite5†Regularization L5: # Training Parameters
L6: The Amazon ML learning algorithm accepts parameters, called hyperparameters or training parameters, that allow you to control the quality of the resulting model. Depending on the hyperparameter, Amazon ML auto-selects settings or provides static defaults for the hyperparameters. Although default hyperparameter settings generally produce useful models, you might be able to improve the predictive performance of your models by changing hyperparameter values.
L7: The following sections describe common hyperparameters associated with learning algorithms for linear models, such as those created by Amazon ML.
L8: ## Learning Rate
L9: The learning rate is a constant value used in the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm. Learning rate affects the speed at which the algorithm reaches (converges to) the optimal weights. The SGD algorithm makes updates to the weights of the linear model for every data example it sees. The size of these updates is controlled by the learning rate. Too large a learning rate might prevent the weights from approaching the optimal solution.
L10: Too small a value results in the algorithm requiring many passes to approach the optimal weights.
L11: In Amazon ML, the learning rate is auto-selected based on your data.
L12: ## Model Size
L13: 
L14: If you have many input features, the number of possible patterns in the data can result in a large model. Large models have practical implications, such as requiring more RAM to hold the model while training and when generating predictions. In Amazon ML, you can reduce the model size by using L1 regularization or by specifically restricting the model size by specifying the maximum size. Note that if you reduce the model size too much, you could reduce your model's predictive power.
L15: For information about the default model size, see cite6†Training Parameters: Types and Default Values . For more information about regularization, see cite5†Regularization .
L16: ## Number of Passes
L17: The SGD algorithm makes sequential passes over the training data. The `Number of passes` parameter controls the number of passes that the algorithm makes over the training data. More passes result in a model that fits the data better (if the learning rate is not too large), but the benefit diminishes with an increasing number of passes. For smaller data sets, you can significantly increase the number of passes, which allows the learning algorithm to effectively fit the data more closely.
L18: For extremely large datasets, a single pass might suffice.
L19: For information about the default number of passes, see cite6†Training Parameters: Types and Default Values .
L20: ## Data Shuffling
L21: In Amazon ML, you must shuffle your data because the SGD algorithm is influenced by the order of the rows in the training data. Shuffling your training data results in better ML models because it helps the SGD algorithm avoid solutions that are optimal for the first type of data it sees, but not for the full range of data. Shuffling mixes up the order of your data so that the SGD algorithm doesn't encounter one type of data for too many observations in succession.
L22: If it sees only one type of data for many successive weight updates, the algorithm might not be able to correct the model weights for a new data type because the update might be too large. Additionally, when the data isn't presented randomly, it's difficult for the algorithm to find the optimal solution for all of the data types quickly; in some cases, the algorithm might never find the optimal solution. Shuffling the training data helps the algorithm to converge on the optimal solution sooner.
L23: For example, say you want to train an ML model to predict a product type, and your training data includes movie, toy, and video game product types. If you sort the data by the product type column before uploading the data to Amazon S3, then the algorithm sees the data alphabetically by product type. The algorithm sees all of your data for movies first, and your ML model begins to learn patterns for movies.
L24: Then, when your model encounters data on toys, every update that the algorithm makes would fit the model to the toy product type, even if those updates degrade the patterns that fit movies. This sudden switch from movie to toy type can produce a model that doesn't learn how to predict product types accurately.
L25: For information about the default shuffling type, see cite6†Training Parameters: Types and Default Values .
L26: ## Regularization
L27: Regularization helps prevent linear models from overfitting training data examples (that is, memorizing patterns instead of generalizing them) by penalizing extreme weight values. L1 regularization has the effect of reducing the number of features used in the model by pushing to zero the weights of features that would otherwise have small weights. As a result, L1 regularization results in sparse models and reduces the amount of noise in the model.
L28: L2 regularization results in smaller overall weight values, and stabilizes the weights when there is high correlation between the input features. You control the amount of L1 or L2 regularization applied by using the `Regularization type` and `Regularization amount` parameters. An extremely large regularization value could result in all features having zero weights, preventing a model from learning patterns.
L29: For information about the default regularization values, see cite6†Training Parameters: Types and Default Values .

L4: cite1†Deserializer cite2†Schema cite3†Serializer L5: # Convert input data format in Amazon Data Firehose
L6: Amazon Data Firehose can convert the format of your input data from JSON to cite4†Apache Parquet†parquet.apache.org or cite5†Apache ORC†orc.apache.org before storing the data in Amazon S3. Parquet and ORC are columnar data formats that save space and enable faster queries compared to row-oriented formats like JSON. If you want to convert an input format other than JSON, such as comma-separated values (CSV) or structured text, you can use AWS Lambda to transform it to JSON first.
L7: For more information, see cite6†Transform source data in Amazon Data Firehose .
L8: You can convert the format of your data even if you aggregate your records before sending them to Amazon Data Firehose.
L9: 
L10: Amazon Data Firehose requires the following three elements to convert the format of your record data:
L11: ## Deserializer
L12: 
L13: Amazon Data Firehose requires a deserializer to read the JSON of your input data. You can choose one of the following two types of deserializer.
L14: 
L15: When combining multiple JSON documents into the same record, make sure that your input is still presented in the supported JSON format. An array of JSON documents is not a valid input.
L16: 
L17: For example, this is the correct input: `{"a": 1}{"b": 1}` and this is the incorrect input: `[{"a":1}, {"a":2}]`.
L18:   * cite7†Apache Hive JSON SerDe†cwiki.apache.org L19: 
L20:   * cite8†OpenX JSON SerDe†github.com L21: 
L22: Choose the cite8†OpenX JSON SerDe†github.com if your input JSON contains time stamps in the following formats:
L23: 
L24:   * yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss[.S]'Z', where the fraction can have up to 9 digits – For example, `2017-02-07T15:13:01.39256Z`.
L25: 
L26:   * yyyy-[M]M-[d]d HH:mm:ss[.S], where the fraction can have up to 9 digits – For example, `2017-02-07 15:13:01.14`.
L27: 
L28:   * Epoch seconds – For example, `1518033528`.
L29:   * Epoch milliseconds – For example, `1518033528123`.
L30: 
L31:   * Floating point epoch seconds – For example, `1518033528.123`.
L32: 
L33: The OpenX JSON SerDe can convert periods (`.`) to underscores (`_`). It can also convert JSON keys to lowercase before deserializing them. For more information about the options that are available with this deserializer through Amazon Data Firehose, see cite9†OpenXJsonSerDe .
L34: If you're not sure which deserializer to choose, use the OpenX JSON SerDe, unless you have time stamps that it doesn't support.
L35: 
L36: If you have time stamps in formats other than those listed previously, use the cite7†Apache Hive JSON SerDe†cwiki.apache.org . When you choose this deserializer, you can specify the time stamp formats to use. To do this, follow the pattern syntax of the Joda-Time `DateTimeFormat` format strings. For more information, see cite10†Class DateTimeFormat†www.joda.org .
L37: You can also use the special value `millis` to parse time stamps in epoch milliseconds. If you don't specify a format, Amazon Data Firehose uses `java.sql.Timestamp::valueOf` by default.
L38: 
L39: The Hive JSON SerDe doesn't allow the following:
L40: 
L41:   * Periods (`.`) in column names.
L42: 
L43:   * Fields whose type is `uniontype`.
L44: 
L45:   * Fields that have numerical types in the schema, but that are strings in the JSON. For example, if the schema is (an int), and the JSON is `{"a":"123"}`, the Hive SerDe gives an error.
L46: The Hive SerDe doesn't convert nested JSON into strings. For example, if you have `{"a":{"inner":1}}`, it doesn't treat `{"inner":1}` as a string.
L47: ## Schema
L48: 
L49: Amazon Data Firehose requires a schema to determine how to interpret that data. Use cite11†AWS Glue to create a schema in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Amazon Data Firehose then references that schema and uses it to interpret your input data. You can use the same schema to configure both Amazon Data Firehose and your analytics software. For more information, see cite12†Populating the AWS Glue Data Catalog in the AWS Glue Developer Guide.
L50: ###### Note
L51: 
L52: The schema created in AWS Glue Data Catalog should match the input data structure. Otherwise, the converted data will not contain attributes that are not specified in the schema. If you use nested JSON, use a STRUCT type in the schema that mirrors the structure of your JSON data. See cite13†this example for how to handle nested JSON with a STRUCT type.
L53: ###### Important
L54: 
L55: For data types that do not specify a size limit, there is a practical limit of 32 MBs for all of the data in a single row.
L56: 
L57: If you specify length for `CHAR` or `VARCHAR`, Firehose truncates the strings at the specified length when it reads the input data. If the underlying data string is longer, it remains unchanged.
L58: ## Serializer
L59: 
L60: Firehose requires a serializer to convert the data to the target columnar storage format (Parquet or ORC) – You can choose one of the following two types of serializers.
L61: 
L62:   * cite14†ORC SerDe†cwiki.apache.org L63: 
L64:   * cite15†Parquet SerDe†cwiki.apache.org L65: 
L66: The serializer that you choose depends on your business needs. To learn more about the two serializer options, see cite14†ORC SerDe†cwiki.apache.org and cite15†Parquet SerDe†cwiki.apache.org .

L2: Managing lexicons - Amazon Polly
L3: # Managing lexicons
L4: 
L5: Pronunciation lexicons enable you to customize the pronunciation of words. Amazon Polly provides API operations that you can use to store lexicons in an AWS region. Those lexicons are then specific to that particular region. You can use one or more of the lexicons from that region when synthesizing the text by using the `SynthesizeSpeech` operation. This applies the specified lexicon to the input text before the synthesis begins. For more information, see cite1†SynthesizeSpeech .
L6: ###### Note
L7: 
L8: These lexicons must conform with the Pronunciation Lexicon Specification (PLS) W3C recommendation. For more information, see cite2†Pronunciation Lexicon Specification (PLS) Version 1.0†www.w3.org on the W3C website.
L9: 
L10: The following are examples of ways to use lexicons with speech synthesis engines:
L11:   * Common words are sometimes stylized with numbers taking the place of letters, as with "g3t sm4rt" (get smart). Humans can read these words correctly. However, a Text-to-Speech (TTS) engine reads the text literally, pronouncing the name exactly as it is spelled. This is where you can leverage lexicons to customize the synthesized speech by using Amazon Polly. In this example, you can specify an alias (get smart) for the word "g3t sm4rt" in the lexicon.
L12:   * Your text might include an acronym, such as W3C. You can use a lexicon to define an alias for the word W3C so that it is read in the full, expanded form (World Wide Web Consortium).
L13: 
L14: Lexicons give you additional control over how Amazon Polly pronounces words uncommon to the selected language. For example, you can specify the pronunciation using a phonetic alphabet. For more information, see cite2†Pronunciation Lexicon Specification (PLS) Version 1.0†www.w3.org on the W3C website.

L6: You can monitor Amazon SageMaker AI using Amazon CloudWatch, which collects raw data and processes it into readable, near real-time metrics. These statistics are kept for 15 months. With them, you can access historical information and gain a better perspective on how your web application or service is performing. However, the Amazon CloudWatch console limits the search to metrics that were updated in the last 2 weeks. This limitation ensures that the most current jobs are shown in your namespace.
L7: To graph metrics without using a search, specify its exact name in the source view. You can also set alarms that watch for certain thresholds, and send notifications or take actions when those thresholds are met. For more information, see the cite10†Amazon CloudWatch User Guide .
L8: ###### SageMaker AI Metrics and Dimensions
L9: 
L10:   * cite1†SageMaker AI endpoint metrics L11: 
L12:   * cite2†SageMaker AI endpoint invocation metrics L13:
